items.model_answer:
If Germany had secured a sustainable wartime supply of food, oil, and rubber despite the Allied blockade, the strategic trajectory of World War II would likely have shifted significantly—but not automatically toward a German victory.

The Allied blockade was a central pillar of Britain’s war strategy. Germany historically suffered chronic shortages of oil, fats, grain, and especially natural rubber, forcing heavy reliance on synthetic substitutes and territorial conquest (Romanian oil, Ukrainian grain). These shortages constrained mobility, limited training and air operations, weakened civilian morale, and forced risky offensives aimed at resource capture—most notably the invasion of the Soviet Union with its eye on Caucasian oil. If Germany had secured reliable external supplies—through guaranteed access to neutral markets, protected sea lanes, or a stable Eurasian resource network—the strategic pressure driving many of its most desperate decisions would have eased.

With abundant oil, the Wehrmacht could have sustained longer air campaigns, expanded pilot training, and maintained mechanized offensives without the chronic fuel rationing that crippled operations after 1942. The Luftwaffe’s declining pilot quality and sortie rates were closely tied to fuel scarcity. A well-fueled German military would have been more capable of prolonged strategic bombing, stronger defense against Allied air superiority, and more resilient responses during campaigns such as North Africa and the Eastern Front.

Reliable rubber supplies would have strengthened vehicle production and maintenance, increasing logistical flexibility. Food security would have reduced domestic strain and improved morale, potentially limiting labor unrest and the need for harsh extraction policies in occupied territories that fueled resistance movements.

Most consequentially, with secure oil supplies, Germany might not have needed to prioritize the 1942 drive toward the Caucasus or overextend itself in resource-driven offensives. A Germany less constrained by scarcity might have fought a more defensive, attritional war after early victories—consolidating gains in Europe and forcing the Allies into a longer, more costly reconquest.

However, several constraints would still remain. First, industrial capacity: by 1943–44, the United States vastly outproduced Germany in ships, aircraft, vehicles, and munitions. Even without resource shortages, Germany faced an overwhelming material imbalance. Second, Allied codebreaking, strategic bombing, and growing Soviet manpower would still exert enormous pressure. Third, ideological and strategic miscalculations—such as the decision to invade the Soviet Union and the genocidal occupation policies that fueled partisan warfare—were not simply products of resource scarcity.

In the best-case scenario for Germany, sustainable supplies might have prolonged the war considerably, possibly forcing a negotiated settlement in Europe if Allied casualties mounted and public support wavered. A more stable German war economy could have delayed collapse on both Eastern and Western fronts, perhaps preventing the rapid disintegration of 1944–45.

But outright Axis victory would still have required defeating or neutralizing both the Soviet Union and the United States—an enormous task even with adequate resources. American industrial supremacy and Soviet manpower reserves were structural advantages that resource sufficiency alone would not erase.

In sum, a Germany free from blockade-induced shortages would likely have fought longer, more effectively, and at greater cost to the Allies. The war might have extended years beyond 1945 or ended in a negotiated division of Europe. Yet resource security, while critical, would not automatically overcome the deep economic and strategic asymmetries that ultimately determined the war’s outcome.

items.question: What If nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a practical reactor to be built around the 1900s?
human_answers: Well, according to Google "Canada's first CANDU prototype, the Nuclear Power Demonstration (NPD) reactor, required a significant amount of heavy water (D2O) for its moderator and coolant, generally around 1 tonne of heavy water per megawatt (MW) of capacity, translating to roughly 20-25 tonnes for its small 20 MWe output..." and "In the 1930's Norwegian company Norsk Hydro began industrial-scale extraction of heavy water (deuterium oxide) at its Vemork plant in Rjukan, using electrolysis as a byproduct of fertilizer production, " Finally from Wikipedia (yes, I know this may well be nonsense) "It was the world's first site to mass-produce heavy water (as a byproduct of nitrogen fixing), with a capacity of 1.2 tonnes per year. " So, by the late 1930's / early 1940's it might well be possible to build a 1 or 2MW CANDU stream generator using just one or two years production from the single Norsk Hydro plant. I assume Canadian hydro plants were built with higher capacity since they (the Canadians) managed to build commercial output (GW) plants requiring 200-300 tones of heavy water in a 'reasonable' timescale (ie. less than 200 years )

Believe it or not, my first engineering degree was in Nuclear Engineering (it was a dead field when I graduated 30 plus years ago, and still is, so I got another degree in Manufacturing Engineering). Yes, you can run reactors with natural enrichment, and the right neutron moderator - heavy water (as in the water molecules have Deuterium instead of your usual one proton no neutrons hydrogen) or graphite come to mind. Both would avoid the need to enrich the fuel (which is a major hassle to do). BUT, that's only part of the story - you need the instrumentation for monitoring the nuclear reactions (to make sure they're occurring, and not getting out of control) which is basically electronic in nature (sorry mechanical won't cut it). In the early 1900s, the field of electronics was embryonic at best. Then there's the material science aspect - you need materials seriously capable of dealing with the high reactor temperatures, and radiation effects (oh yeah, and the material can't interfere excessively with the neutron flux, which would disrupt the reaction) - sorry not happening, material science was in its infancy IMO. There is also the safety aspect - you need shielding for any radiation emitted from the reactor. The health aspects of radiation exposure were basically unknown, resulting in many people getting exposed to and dying of cancer (Marie Curie, early X-Ray technicians, the so called "Radium Girls" who painted the glowing dots on watch faces). In certain cases of extreme exposure (due to reactor surges, etc.), you can die from the radiation days after the exposure. In short, IMO, having a viable nuclear reactor in the early 1900s is a non-starter.

To your first part: Fair enough. It seems like this might require ASB, like just magically gifting people the entire lexicon of nuclear understanding and teaching them how to make purer graphite. I'm not sure I entirely agree with the second part. Were the engineers that built the Chicago Pile doing sophisticated core analysis? Did they know the neutron flux? I feel like you could "fly blind" and just go by heat/steam output, especially since "won't immediately melt down and ruin my investment" is probably considered sufficient by 1900s standards of safety (especially if the health effects of radiation are not yet understood). Granted, it seems very, very likely that the long term effects of this mentality would make for a much more radioactively contaminated world... Ah, but I didn't say for generating electricity, per se. A nuclear boiler just for steam would be useful. And I doubt they'd come up with a design that requires steam generators or controlling boron concentration in the coolant: I wouldn't expect anything like a PWR with its separation between a primary and secondary loop. More like a BWR or RBMK, where the radioactive steam is directly used. If the objective is electricity, it may require a bit longer than early 1900s. But by the time you have coal plants coming online, you have everything you need for the conventional thermal plant.

To elaborate on some things: as far as I can tell, there are possibly 3 historical reactor designs that used unenriched/natural uranium: heavy-water moderated CANDU reactors, graphite-moderated gas-cooled reactors (Magnox and UNGG), and possibly the graphite-moderated Soviet RBMK reactors (although RBMK reactors typically used low-enriched uranium). Heavy water's out of the question; it was only discovered in the 1930s, and even WW2-era methods for extracting heavy water were massively energy-intensive. NPD, the first CANDU reactor producing some 20 MW of electricity, required 28,660kg of heavy water. Using pure electrolysis to extract the heavy water - the initial method used to extract heavy water at Vemork - required about 58,000 kilowatt hours per pound of heavy water, or 3.6 billion kilowatt-hours to produce all the necessary heavy water. As a quick comparison, the US' entire monthly electricity generation in April 1922 was about 3.6 billion kilowatt hours. That means the NPD reactor, if it obtained heavy water using pre-WW2 methods, could run for 20 years straight and not break even on the power needed to create the heavy water necessary to run the plant (not to mention some heavy water will be lost in operation) before the development of postwar heavy water production methods. UNGG and RBMK definitely used zirconium cladding for their fuel elements (necessary because zirconium has a smaller neutron absorption cross-section and is resistant to corrosion); the issue is that metal zirconium wasn't commercially synthesized until 1925, and it wasn't commercially synthesized cheaply until after WW2. The specific zirconium alloys used in the fuel claddings weren't developed until the postwar either. RBMK reactors operate with water at pressures of about 1,000 psi; that wasn't achieved by land-based power generation systems until 1925. Uranium metal used in the gas-cooled reactors is difficult to work with considering it corrodes a lot of metals when molten, thus requiring graphite molds of decently high purity (maybe not as pure as nuclear graphite, but boron has to be minimized). Also the furnaces used to cast the uranium were vacuum induction furnaces, a technology not invented until the 1920s. Turning the uranium metal into fuel rods that can be inserted also required a ton of research and development to the point where it was once considered the most critical job at Hanford for the Manhattan Project.
items.original_question: What if A nuclear reactor, four decades early? I posit that with the technology of the early 1900s, a nuclear reactor could've been theoretically possible had the theory been understood. Uranium enrichment is entirely out of the question, but not all reactor designs require it. The industrialists of the 1900s had access to graphite, yellowcake, and boron, which would allow the creation and control of a graphite-moderated natural uranium reactor, so long as the graphite was pure enough (I am admittedly unsure if that level of purity would be possible, but I am presuming so given what little I know of the process). Is there any plausible scenario where the discovery of nuclear fission is pushed back far enough for our enterprising titans of industry to begin harnessing nuclear steam, short of dropping off a modern nuclear physics textbook in their engineers' laps? If so, what effects would this have on the world?

items.model_answer:
If nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a practical reactor to be built around 1900, the political, military, and economic trajectory of the 20th century would likely have changed dramatically—but not in a simple or uniformly transformative way.

First, the scientific and industrial context matters. Around 1900, physics was still developing the foundations of atomic theory. Even if fission had been identified and chain reactions engineered, scaling reactors would have required advances in materials science, precision engineering, and large-scale industrial coordination. The most likely early adopters would have been major industrial powers—Britain, Germany, France, and the United States—because they had the scientific institutions and capital required. Nuclear power would initially have been state-driven and tightly linked to military and naval ambitions.

One immediate impact would likely have been on naval power. Coal was central to imperial logistics; fleets depended on coaling stations across empires. Nuclear-powered ships—even if primitive—would have radically reduced refueling needs and altered the strategic value of colonial ports. The British Empire, whose power relied heavily on coal logistics, might have retained naval supremacy longer if it mastered nuclear propulsion early. Alternatively, if Germany gained an early lead, it could have shifted the naval balance before World War I.

World War I itself could have unfolded differently. If reactors existed by the 1910s, they might initially have served as stationary power sources for industry and rail electrification rather than weapons. However, once fission was understood, the possibility of atomic bombs would have followed sooner or later. Given the intense arms race atmosphere before 1914, there is a real possibility that nuclear weapons research would have begun during or immediately after World War I. If atomic bombs had appeared in the 1910s or 1920s, their first use might have been in a far less restrained strategic culture than that of 1945. The norms and taboos that developed after Hiroshima did not exist earlier, and mass bombing of civilians was already becoming normalized during World War I. An earlier nuclear age might therefore have been even more destabilizing.

Economically, early nuclear power could have reduced dependence on coal decades earlier. This might have slowed the growth of oil geopolitics, potentially reducing the strategic centrality of the Middle East. Electrification could have expanded faster, especially in Europe, if reactors provided abundant base-load power. On the other hand, early reactors would likely have been expensive and centralized, reinforcing state control over energy rather than democratizing it.

In terms of environmental effects, earlier nuclear adoption might have reduced cumulative carbon emissions over the 20th century by displacing some coal burning. However, without modern safety culture and regulatory frameworks, accidents and radiation exposure could have been more frequent and poorly managed, possibly creating public backlash or localized disasters.

Politically, the existence of nuclear weapons before or during World War I could have either deterred large-scale war or made it catastrophically shorter and more destructive. If one power achieved a temporary monopoly, it might have reshaped the international order decisively—perhaps preventing the prolonged stalemate of trench warfare but at the cost of immense destruction in a few cities. Alternatively, rapid proliferation among rival empires could have made preemptive war more likely in a highly unstable multipolar system.

Overall, an early discovery of practical fission around 1900 would probably have accelerated both the centralization of state power and the scale of destructive capability. The 20th century might have seen nuclear geopolitics emerge not after two world wars but before or during the first—potentially making the era either more quickly stabilized through deterrence or even more violently transformative in its opening decades.

items.question: Skywalker Ranch Foundation: What If Lucasfilm Was Never Sold to Disney
human_answers: Lucas didn’t expend much effort in assembling the rest of the Creative Council. It was mostly a collection of people who had defined Lucasfilm properties for a generation. The first member was Kiri Hart, Lucasfilm’s resident surveyor of canon. Doug Chiang was the second to agree. He had created the stunning visual spectacles that were Naboo and Coruscant in The Phantom Menace. He had made the prequels more mythic in appearance than the originals and that was someone Filoni felt this new Foundation needed. Kathleen Kennedy was the last member. She had overseen the creation of many classics, mostly outside of Lucasfilm. Even if that wasn’t the case, Filoni could not pretend there wasn’t a corporate aspect to the Foundation. The corporation was what would keep the Foundation propped up. Filoni felt both eager to get underway and terrified about what would happen in this meeting. Lucas had essentially anointed him his successor. There was a lot to live up to, but Filoni trusted Lucas’ judgement and that was the only consolation he could come up with. Filoni walked into the boardroom and he clapped his hands. “Hey, everyone. Thank you for coming”, he said. The creators nodded in Filoni’s direction as he sat down. Doug pushed his notepad to the centre of the desk as Kiri closed her binder full of canon notes. “I know what you’re thinking. This is new territory for me too. But, let’s see how this pans out”, Filoni replied. The creators didn’t respond. “Our mandate is clear. We have the responsibility to protect what Lucasfilm stands for. We need to tell new stories while protecting what the old ones stand for”, As some of the creators shifted position in their seats, Dave continued. “This is about the generations of people who see Lucasfilm as the pillar of mythic entertainment”, he said. “What do we do first?” Kennedy asked. “The Foundation goes public in October. Before then, I want a clear statement of what the Foundation will stand for. We don’t want our fans to have any doubt about our integrity”, Kiri nodded, but asked. “What is our integrity? What do we stand for?” Dave looked around the table. “We stand for storytelling and for what it can bring to the world”, he said. “That is a noble goal, Dave. But we can’t forget that part of this Foundation is a business. We need to operate within current and upcoming industries. We need to form connections”, Kennedy replied. Doug then replied. “I don’t think Dave is forgetting that, but we need to tell the industry that we decide what stories are told. Too many stories are being decided in high rise boardrooms”, Filoni nodded. “Exactly. There is a balance we need to respect”, he said. “Creative sovereignty will be our first pillar then. We will work with the industry, but we won’t let them rewrite our stories to fit social media trends”, Kiri replied. Dave nodded in her direction. “We also need to figure out a commercially viable way to support new creators. Are we going to let everyone with a camera and dream camp outside of Skywalker Ranch and hope for their shot?” Kennedy asked. “Once we work out that process, how do we protect their work?” she continued. “Okay, so we’ve decided on our values. Creative sovereignty, visual and emotional integrity and creator support”, Dave said as he counted the values on his fingers. “Who wants to work on the statement?” he called out. Kiri and Doug stood up. “We’ll get it started”, Dave nodded as he looked at Kennedy. “I’ll get the production framework going”, she said. Filoni laid back in his seat. This first meeting was remarkably painless, but he suspected this was where the ease of the job ended. Comments We are a long way off from dealing with the sequels, but they will be addressed eventually. I will be preserving the Mandalorian, since that was Filoni's pet project for a while. And yes, Lucasfilm will be retaining their relationship with Disney. If there is something like Galaxy's Edge, it won't be entirely based around the sequels.
items.original_question: Skywalker Ranch Foundation: What if Lucasfilm Was Never Sold to Disney (I originally intended for this to be a timeline which would've covered the production of a Clone Wars-style animated series set in a different version of the sequel trilogy, but when I determined that Disney was too business oriented to create something like what I was making, I went back to the drawing board and I came up with this instead. This will be my first production timeline so I may or may not update this on the regular, but I wanted to do something to mark the 10th anniversary of The Force Awakens) Anyway, sound off on what you think. # June 2012 “Well done, everybody!” Dave Filoni shouted when he saw the final animation of The Wrong Jedi, the last episode of The Clone Wars Season 5. There was loud applause from across the room. Filoni looked back towards George Lucas. He could’ve sworn he saw a tear in the old man’s eye. The Clone Wars was out for another season. The final step was to send the seasons to Cartoon Network to show the fans. Filoni thought this was probably the best season yet. He wasn’t surprised since he knew he had the best team in the business working alongside him. But, the celebration couldn’t last forever. He had to work with his team on the next season. Lucas had been a felt absence through the production of Season 5, but he had his input on scripts he thought were special. Filoni smiled as he wondered how long he could keep luring Lucas back to Skywalker Ranch. Before the team could leave, Lucas called out. “Before you leave, I have an announcement to make”, he said. The team turned to face Lucas, but Lucas raised his hand. “Not here. Let’s go somewhere less shadowy”, he said. Lucas led his team out of the Ranch proper and towards the artificially created lake that sat in the middle of the Skywalker Ranch complex. Filoni was never tired of the verdant paradise that Skywalker Ranch was. “Alright, George. What’s up?” Filoni asked with a brief smile. Lucas looked to his fellow creators and took a deep breath. “I don’t know what to say, so I am just going to come right out and say it. I will be stepping down from Lucasfilm at the end of the year”, The creators looked at each other. Lucas’s felt absence suddenly made sense. There was no shock or gasp of surprise. Instead, there was a quiet acknowledgement. “Are you sure you want that?” Filoni asked. “Yes. I’ve been thinking about it for about a year. I’ve told my stories and I want to spend the rest of my life with my family”, “Who’s going to take over?” Kliner asked. “Kathleen Kennedy is going to be handling the corporate side of things, but that’s not why I called you here”, Lucas continued. The shock of the news that one of Spielberg’s top collaborators was going to run Lucasfilm briefly subsided as they waited for Lucas. “I’ve been considering what to do with this alliance that I’ve spent the better part of my life putting together. When I first built this place, I had just dodged a bullet when A New Hope smashed the box office. I’ve put my life and my psyche on the line to not only make art for people to enjoy, but to make an environment where filmmakers can tell their stories”, Lucas said as he stretched out his arms to take in the entirety of the Ranch. “You’ve certainly accomplished that”, Athena Portillo said to everyone’s agreement. “I’ve considered selling all of this to Disney. They have reach that I can only dream of, but I’ve had my doubts”, he said as he turned around from the lake. “When I first became a filmmaker, I hated the studio system. They were all hacks who made films based on what was popular at the time. I’m not saying Disney is a company full of hacks, but I don’t want their corporate attitudes diluting what I, Gary, Ralph, Ben and Maria created thirty years ago. I want this place to remain pure”, Lucas continued. “I’m sorry, George, but what are you trying to say?” Kliner asked. Lucas exhaled. “I’ve talked with Kathy and Brennan. They were reluctant at first, but they’ve agreed to keep Lucasfilm as an independent entity. Not only that, but they’ve agreed to begin laying the groundwork for the Skywalker Ranch Foundation”, “And what is that?” Filoni asked. “It is what is going to keep Lucasfilm in the public consciousness for the next decade or so. It is going to protect the integrity of everything we’ve made here. Not just Star Wars, but Indiana Jones, Willow and everything else that has this place’s name on it. Nobody will be able to touch the properties inside this building until they can prove they can do the work necessary to preserve it”, Before the creators could ask further questions, Lucas continued. “But the Foundation will also produce new content that fits what this place stands for. We’re still putting the infrastructure together, but it will produce new content outside of the studio system, just like back when the original trilogy was being produced”, “Who’s going to lead this Foundation?” Filoni asked. “Like I said, Kathy is going to lead the corporate side of it, but she won’t be the voice of the Foundation. The Foundation will be led by creators”, Lucas replied. He then looked towards Dave and walked towards him. “When you first joined Lucasfilm in 2008, I was surprised by how connected you were to what this company stood for. You weren’t just a director, you were a storyteller through and through. That’s the kind of person I need keeping the Ranch intact. I want you to be the first leader of the Creative Council”, Dave felt his cheeks turning red. He suddenly felt like he had been pulled back in time to when he first joined Lucasfilm. He thought that had been a joke at first. This didn’t feel like a joke. This was something Dave couldn’t put into words. “You want me to be in charge of your legacy? George, I’m flattered, but that’s a whole different thing from making a TV show”, Dave pointed out. “Just keep the story straight. That will be your job. You will have other creators working alongside you on the Council and these people will stay on to help you in the trenches”, Lucas reassured him as he pointed to the creators, some of whom Filoni had known since he first joined the company. The creators watched as Dave looked out across the water. He could’ve sworn Binary Sunset was playing in the back of his head. This was his threshold. He thought he had crossed that line in 2008, but he had been wrong. Lucas wasn’t just trusting him with his story, he was trusting him with what Lucasfilm was going to stand for after he was gone. Dave separated himself from the real world for a moment. He saw X Wings and TIE Fighters flying over the Ranch, he could hear the ethereal hum of lightsabers and finally, he heard Yoda’s famous phrase. “Do or do not. There is no try”, Filoni turned around. “I’ll do it”, he said which led to applause from his fellow creators and Lucas shaking his hand. “Lucasfilm couldn’t be in better hands”, Lucas simply said.

items.model_answer:
If Lucasfilm had never been sold to Disney in 2012, the trajectory of both *Star Wars* and the broader media landscape would likely look very different. Under continued independent ownership—presumably still guided by George Lucas or a closely aligned creative leadership structure—Lucasfilm would probably have remained a smaller, more creatively centralized studio focused on long-term storytelling rather than rapid franchise expansion.

First, the sequel trilogy as released (Episodes VII–IX) almost certainly would not exist in its current form. George Lucas had his own outlines for sequels centered more on midichlorians, the Whills, and the rebuilding of the Republic. These concepts were reportedly more philosophical and exploratory than the nostalgia-driven approach Disney adopted. Without Disney’s corporate mandate for a tentpole revival, any continuation of the saga would likely have been slower, more experimental, and potentially more divisive—but also more unified in vision.

Second, the scale and speed of franchise expansion would have been far smaller. Disney turned *Star Wars* into a multi-platform streaming ecosystem with series like *The Mandalorian*, *Andor*, *Ahsoka*, and others feeding Disney+. An independent Lucasfilm might have produced occasional films or high-quality television projects, but not at the volume or frequency seen after 2015. The brand would likely feel less saturated and more event-driven, with longer gaps between major releases.

Third, merchandising and global integration would be less aggressive. Disney’s synergy machine—theme park expansions like Galaxy’s Edge, extensive cross-brand licensing, and global marketing saturation—dramatically expanded *Star Wars* as a commercial empire. Without that infrastructure, the franchise would still be lucrative but less omnipresent in global consumer culture. It might retain more of a niche, cult-epic identity rather than functioning as a pillar of one of the world’s largest entertainment conglomerates.

Creatively, Lucasfilm might have taken greater formal risks. George Lucas historically prioritized technological innovation and experimental storytelling over market expectations. A non-Disney Lucasfilm could have invested further in digital production technologies or niche storytelling experiments, perhaps through the Skywalker Ranch Foundation or educational and artistic initiatives. However, financial risk tolerance would be lower without Disney’s capital reserves, limiting blockbuster-scale projects.

Culturally, fan polarization might look different. The Disney era triggered debates over canon resets, legacy character treatment, and corporate storytelling. Under Lucas, controversies would still exist—given reactions to the prequels—but they would stem from auteur decisions rather than corporate franchise management. The brand might feel more singular, for better or worse.

Finally, Disney itself would be in a weaker franchise position without *Star Wars*. The acquisition strengthened Disney’s dominance alongside Marvel and Pixar. Without it, streaming competition and franchise diversification strategies might have evolved differently.

In summary, if Lucasfilm had never been sold, *Star Wars* would likely be smaller in scale, slower in output, more centralized in creative control, and potentially more experimental—but less globally ubiquitous. The franchise might feel more cohesive and auteur-driven, yet less commercially expansive and culturally omnipresent.

items.question: What If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon for crewed lunar missions?
human_answers: I don't think you understand SpaceX very well. The Starship "failures" are the result of rapid design-test-redesign, pushing the hardware to its limits to find out just what those limits actually are. I think they are up to the third generation design. If putting a Starship into orbit was so important to them, they'd have done by now. Still in test phase. Falcon 9 (and Heavy) is not about putting maximum mass into space, it is about putting payloads into space at minimum cost. So yes, a single type of engine and propellant all the way to orbit: the upper stage is just a cut-down version of the launcher and Merlin Vacuum is a Merlin 1D with a longer nozzle for more efficiency. Reusing a booster cuts payload mass by about 40%, but they break-even on the second or third flight. Falcon 9 is so cost-efficient that SpaceX is eating everyone else's lunch at this point. It's no Saturn V, to be sure, but it isn't meant to be. Saturn V was designed with each stage optimized just for its specific part of the mission... which made it extremely expensive to develop and build and totally uneconomic. A diametrically opposite design approach.

I actually like the idea of an improved dragon better than what we have with Starship (assuming it ever carries humans). As for using it for lunar missions. Do we need to recreate the Apollo Mission profile or can we build some sort of transfer craft a sort of tug or booster that can be docked with and used to get to and from the moon. We would need a way to refuel it in earth orbit but it may be one way to get Dragon to the moon. And long term it may be better. I have always thought that we needed some sort of “space craft” vs the way we do everything with the vehicle we use to get up and down from earth. That would I suppose be a big task to build and maintain and refuel this transfer vehicle. But it may allow a less powerful system to do the job. And once you have the hardware it is harder to cancel the thing. So we may actually get some long term use.

All true of course, also fully ignored in most cases and specifically in the articles/videos I cited above The "mantra" is simply that Dragon is cheaper and therefor better than Orion. Similar statements about Falcon versus SLS. One of the videos I didn't cite was in fact one that suggests Lunar HLS "Starship" will be used for ferrying the landing party from LEO to LLO where they would use Dragon to land on the Moon and then return to the HLS "Starship" to be ferried back to LEO where Dragon would be used to land on Earth. Ya, IIRC you lose the core stage. Ya it would be 'neat' but keep in mind the Super Draco's are not actually "throttleable" since they are supposed to be used as abort rockets and not landing rockets. The way the propellants are stored at very high pressures in order to get that high thrust for abort and I think that precludes landing use so they likely would have to be redesigned.. Randy
items.original_question: What if Falcon/Dragon to the Moon? Kind of bouncing off this thread as I've run across some of the usual "hype" sources such as this and this , (nothing from SpaceX though which I think is telling) "bragging" about SpaceX's "great new plan" to send crew Dragon to the Moon "sooner than NASA or China" etc, et-al. (Of course they all simply ignore the issues with Dragon going beyond LEO and the fact Orion and SLS are designed to do exactly that but what would I expect ) So the question is essentially "What if SpaceX had continued to iterate and improve Dragon and Falcon Heavy for use in Lunar missions? Granting that as I pointed out here that there's likely no "place" for such a move since the SpaceX to Mars focus was pretty much baked in since the start and with such a short timeline getting a plausible POD is going to be problematic I do wonder if a bit more focus on "Dear Moon" along with Cargo/Crew Dragon couldn't set up a premise where the eventual "HLS" might end up more realistic? Anyway, open for thoughts and comments Randy

If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon specifically for crewed lunar missions—rather than pivoting its primary focus to Starship—the trajectory of both NASA’s Artemis program and commercial deep‑spaceflight might look significantly different, though with important limitations.

Falcon Heavy, as built, can send substantial mass toward the Moon, but it was never optimized for large, single-launch lunar architectures. To support crewed lunar missions, SpaceX would likely have pursued a multi‑launch, Earth‑orbit rendezvous strategy: one or more Falcon Heavy launches to send a modified Dragon and propulsion stage toward lunar orbit, and possibly additional launches to pre‑position fuel or a lunar lander. Crew Dragon itself would have required upgrades for deep‑space radiation protection, extended life support beyond low Earth orbit, and higher‑energy reentry from lunar return velocities. A service module or enhanced trunk with propulsion and power systems—closer to an Apollo-style configuration—would have been necessary.

If this development path had succeeded, SpaceX could have offered NASA an earlier commercial alternative to SLS/Orion for lunar orbit missions, potentially reducing cost per flight and introducing competition into cislunar crew transport. NASA might have used Dragon for lunar flybys or Gateway crew transport while retaining SLS for heavier cargo. This could have accelerated some Artemis timelines in the late 2020s, especially for lunar orbit missions, because Falcon Heavy was operational years before SLS flew successfully.

items.question: What If the Brits had carried out a second attack at Taranto?
human_answers: The only time Aircraft Carriers carry out multi-day attacks on the same location is when they either are providing air cover to an invasion force or have total air superiority. If Pearl Harbour had been a single raid each day for two days the raid on the second day would have suffered serious losses and the patrol aircraft may have located the Carriers which then becomes a very big question of risking a Carrier. Aircraft Carriers are great at projecting power in that they represent overwhelming firepower from unexpected directions at any time. For example look at the exercises carried out between the cold war Royal Navy and the USA. I think it was HMS Ark Royal which involved HMS Ark Royal being the aggressor and striking US bases on the US Eastern Sea Board. up to a week of operations with strikes on a daily basis and undetected due to sneaky sneaky tactics. Aircraft Carriers are also hideously vulnerable to attrition and easily overwhelmed while in contact with shore based aircraft. Naval Aircraft are compromises due to structural needs and limitations caused by operational environment. The exact same engine in an airframe designed with the same technology will result in a land based aircraft of higher basic capability. The further technology has improved the smaller the difference in performance. During 1940's this difference was massive. Size constraints include wingspan, height and weight. Takeoff distance is also important. Range suffers because you need to hit takeoff speed much sooner. What all of this leads to is the fact the Royal Navy could not safely carry out more than a single night of attacks. The Raid was split into two waves due to time it took to launch the loaded aircraft then spot the next wave on the flight deck. Number of aircraft in an attack is also determined by speed at which aircraft could be launched. Even today the raid count is determined by rate of aircraft launch and form up time. j If the Royal Navy had 4 Fleet Carriers available the raid would still have been a single night. However the number of aircraft in each raid would have changed. With 4 carriers the raid would have likely been 80 Swordfish in two waves and it would also have been possible to attempt to wipe out the local airbases in order to do a daylight follow up. The Fighters from 4 Carriers would have been able to fend of larger opposition. If the aircraft compliment was the same as HMS Ilustrious then you could plan on 60 Fulmar's to be available. The likelihood is however that had 4 Carriers been available the air group would be Swordfish, Fulmar's and Sea Gladiators with 60 fighters in Fleet being impossible at this time of the war. 40 Swordfish with Torpedo's and 40 with bombs and flares equals Taranto being removed as a Naval Base for a full year with few Oil storage tanks remaining and the ships in the harbour being severely damaged and total constructive losses. Photos of Taranto pre war show the ships moored stern in at a the docks and essentially tied together. This being hit by 250 or 500lb bombs would decimate the Italian ships due to very week deck armour. 20 to 50 mm is very light and even a 250lb SAP bomb should go through. If 6 ships and tied together you create a 60m by 140m target square as a minimum with plenty of HE and fuel to burn in the ships. Swordfish Dive Bombing was fairly accurate. 40 Torpedo armed and 32 bombers with 8 Flare dropping aircraft equals insane damage levels.

The Brits achieved miracles with a bunch of obsolete biplanes ... The first wave, 12 aircraft, consisted of 6 Swordfish armed with torpedoes, 2 two with flares plus four 250 lb (110 kg) bombs, and 4 with six bombs. The second wave , 8 aircraft, 5 with torpedoes, 2 with flares pus four bombs. Total attack force, 20 aircraft, of which only 11 actually carried a torpedo ! (contrast Pearl Harbor, Japanese attack force= 353 aircraft) The Brits don't need more 'waves', they need more aircraft and more carriers... Which means a POD of 1 April 1918 (April Fools day === how appropriate ) and a replacement of the 'Bomber will always get through' nonsense with one of 'By 1940 our carrier fleet will sink your battleship fleet' (it's debatable when this would be accepted, HOWEVER :- By 1918, the RN had between 650 and 936 Short 184 torpedo bombers. In 1919, the RN had taken delivery of 90 Sopwith Cuckoo torpedo bombers (the had ordered 230 but then the war ended). So, even in 1918, some-one in the RN was having some 'modern' thoughts

items.model_answer:
If the British had carried out a second major air attack on Taranto in late 1940, the strategic balance in the central Mediterranean could have shifted more decisively—and possibly earlier—in Britain’s favor.

The first attack in November 1940 crippled three Italian battleships and demonstrated the vulnerability of capital ships in harbor. However, the Royal Navy did not immediately follow up with a similarly large strike. A second well-executed attack, launched before the Italians had fully repaired defenses and dispersed their fleet, might have sunk or permanently disabled additional major vessels, including heavy cruisers and surviving battleships. This could have reduced the Italian battle fleet to a token force for a prolonged period.

The main consequences would likely have been operational rather than transformative. With the Regia Marina further weakened, British convoys to Malta and Egypt would have faced less surface threat in early 1941. This could have eased supply pressures during the North African campaign and possibly strengthened British positions against Axis advances under Rommel. It might also have reduced the need for risky fleet engagements such as Cape Matapan, or at least tilted them even more decisively toward Britain.

However, there are important limits to the counterfactual. First, Italian naval power was already constrained by fuel shortages and cautious doctrine. Even before Taranto, the Italian fleet rarely sought decisive battle. Second, by 1941 the Luftwaffe’s presence in Sicily and southern Italy increasingly threatened British naval operations. Air power, not surface fleets, became the dominant factor in the central Mediterranean. A second Taranto strike would not have eliminated Axis air superiority in the region.

Politically and psychologically, another successful strike might have deepened the shock to Italy’s prestige and naval morale, possibly encouraging Germany to intervene even more aggressively in the Mediterranean. It also could have accelerated global recognition of carrier-based air power, reinforcing lessons that Japan was already absorbing.

In sum, a second attack at Taranto would probably have further crippled the Italian surface fleet and improved Britain’s operational freedom in the Mediterranean in 1941. It would not have ended the naval war there, but it might have made British logistics to Malta and North Africa more secure at a critical moment, with modest but meaningful strategic consequences.

items.question: What If Vichy France had sent 100,000 French troops to help defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944?
human_answers: When the Allies invaded NW Africa, the French colonies of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia Kesselrings command was approved to recruit patriotic French to resist the Allies. The proposed infantry division never materialized. Enough men were found for a weak battalion, but after the unhealthy and unreliable were rejected there were enough to form a single over strength company. Given the German shortage of up to date equipment, particularly artillery and motor transport. The extra 100,000 French would be armed with the usual mix of older & obsolescent weapons, often in inferior numbers, like most other ground combat formations in Rundsteadts OB West. Just maybe there would be a SS 'Frankreich' division with good equipment, but otherwise its going to be leftovers, horse drawn artillery, little or no medium and heavy artillery, no supporting armor other than a few obsolescent R35 or D2 tanks, pitiful air support, inferior AT guns, French made MG vs the MG 34 or MG42. Compounding all this is the chronic German shortages of artillery ammunition and fuel. If the 100,000 French soldiers are used to offset other soldiers who are then sent to other front the questions is who? The overaged German reservists of the Bodenstang formations? The Ossies from Poland, Urkraine, Beylo Russ, ect... ? The elite Panzer Truppen? If the French are just added on top of the others, with no transfers, then its just the same inadequate equipment spread across a increase of 5% or 10% of men. A second given is the relatively small number of French soldiers who volunteered for the crusade in the east. The members of the Charlemagne division totaled far less than 100,000 through the entire war. Probably less than 50,000 served in that formation. While volunteers could be found to fight in the east, there was no similar movement in the west. The Milcie managed to recruit young men who wanted to avoid labor service, but that relatively large body failed to volunteer or participate in the battle of France. Most deserted long before the Allied armies over ran the police districts the Milcie units were assigned to.

If Vichy France had somehow sent 100,000 French troops to help defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944, the impact would have depended less on numbers alone and more on timing, equipment, morale, and political context. Even so, it likely would not have changed the overall outcome of the Normandy invasion or the war in Western Europe, though it could have made the initial Allied campaign bloodier and slower.

First, the political premise is highly counterfactual. By 1944, Vichy France had effectively ceased to function as an autonomous regime. After Germany occupied the “Free Zone” in 1942, Vichy’s sovereignty was largely symbolic. Raising, equipping, and deploying 100,000 reliable troops under German operational control would have required a level of military rebuilding and collaboration that did not exist. Most Vichy forces had been disbanded or were lightly armed, and loyalty to the regime was uneven at best.

If, however, we assume 100,000 additional French troops were present along the Atlantic Wall in June 1944, several factors matter. The Atlantic Wall’s weakness was not simply manpower but poor mobility, insufficient reserves, weak air cover, and Allied naval and air superiority. Many German units on the coast were static divisions with limited transport. Additional French troops, especially if similarly under-equipped and lacking heavy weapons, would likely have been used as static infantry in coastal defenses. They might have increased resistance on some beaches, particularly at places like Omaha or in secondary sectors, raising Allied casualties during the initial landings.

However, the decisive factors in Normandy were Allied control of the sea and air, logistical superiority, and the ability to build up overwhelming force once a beachhead was secured. Even if 100,000 extra defenders had stiffened the coastal crust, the Allies landed over 150,000 troops on D-Day alone and poured in millions over the following months. Without equivalent armored reserves, artillery, and air support, additional French infantry would probably have been attrited by naval bombardment, air strikes, and sustained ground assaults.

There is also the issue of morale and reliability. Many French soldiers in 1944 were not ideologically committed to Nazi Germany. Some might have surrendered quickly or even defected once confronted by Allied forces, especially given the growing strength of the French Resistance and the legitimacy of Free France under de Gaulle. If morale were low, their military value would be limited. If, in a more extreme counterfactual, they were highly motivated collaborators, they might have fought harder, but this would not compensate for Germany’s strategic disadvantages.

The most plausible effect would have been a delay. The Allies might have taken longer to secure certain beachheads or to break out from Normandy. Casualties on both sides could have been higher, and cities in northern France might have suffered more destruction during prolonged fighting. A delay of weeks, perhaps even a couple of months, is conceivable in a maximal scenario.

But by mid-1944, Germany was already collapsing on the Eastern Front under Soviet offensives, and Allied industrial capacity vastly exceeded that of the Axis. Even a stronger Atlantic Wall would not have reversed these structural realities. At most, it would have made the liberation of France slower and bloodier; it would not have prevented it.

human_answers: In the OTL First World War, aircraft were used only as reconnaissance planes in the early stages, and pilots dropped bombs by hand. However, by the later years of the war, aviation had achieved remarkable progress. Even if they do not appear in the early phase of the First World War in this TL, they could still emerge later in the conflict and be used for roles such as reconnaissance. Germany and its friends would be pleased to hear that. As I understand it, the Haber-Bosch process spread more slowly than people often assume. Fixing nitrogen in a laboratory and mass-producing chemical fertilizer in a factory are entirely different challenges. Building reactors that could withstand pressures of 200 to 300 atmospheres, developing steel alloys that could endure prolonged exposure to high temperature and high pressure, solving catalyst lifespan problems, controlling thermal runaway and explosions, designing continuous processes, and making the system capable of running nonstop for thousands of hours—this was not simply a matter of chemistry, but a comprehensive scientific and engineering project that required physics, materials science, mechanical engineering, and electrical engineering as well. In the 1910s, Germany was the only country in the world capable of doing both. In the OTL, once the Haber process had been developed, the First World War broke out almost immediately. During that period, all resources were directed not toward chemical fertilizer production, but toward the development of explosives. Even afterward, BASF maintained its monopoly over the Haber method.

items.original_question: What if World War I had occurred 9 years earlier? The First Moroccan Crisis occurred between 1905 and 1906 during the Russo-Japanese War. Although this event did not escalate into a full-scale military conflict, it was resolved through the Algeciras Conference. However, tensions between the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente grew stronger. Then, in 1911, the Second Moroccan Crisis took place. At this time, there were talks of a potential war, but ultimately it was resolved through international negotiations. Despite these series of events, in 1914, World War I broke out due to the assassination of the Austrian Archduke and the subsequent invasion of Serbia. This raises an interesting question. During the July Crisis in the OTL, there were numerous efforts to avoid war, but in the end, the arrogance of autocratic monarchs and the complex web of interests caused tensions to escalate and ultimately explode. What if such a chain reaction and explosion had occurred during the First Moroccan Crisis? What if the First Moroccan Crisis had escalated into a full-blown war, leading to World War I happening 9 years earlier than in the OTL? What could have been the consequences of such a scenario? Here are the questions in English: 1. In 1905, how does the military strength of countries such as the United Kingdom, France, the Russian Empire, the German Empire, Austria-Hungary, and the Kingdom of Italy compare to that of 1914 in OTL? Which country would be at a disadvantage compared to OTL when the war begins? 2. In 1905, the ruling party of the United States is the Republican Party, and the president is Theodore Roosevelt. If a world war were to occur during his presidency, what would America's stance be? Would Teddy Roosevelt maintain neutrality throughout, or would he eventually push for involvement? And how would Roosevelt's vision for the post-war world differ from Wilson's? 3. The Russian Empire, after the Russo-Japanese War in OTL, pursued reforms like constitutional monarchy changes and Stolypin’s agricultural reforms. However, in this TL, war breaks out before such reforms happen. What impact do you think this would have on Russia? I believe Russia would be at a disadvantage compared to OTL. However, there is also this possibility: "Unlike in OTL, there would be no Duma, and no legitimate or proper opposition parties. As a result, although there are many opposing forces, they would not form a cohesive alliance, and there would be no single negotiation channel." "This would make it harder for the anti-government factions to gain representation throughout Russia. Therefore, after the revolution, it would be more difficult to quickly take over the government and establish a revolutionary regime." 4. What do you think is the most likely outcome of the world war in this alternate timeline?

If a general European war had broken out around 1905 instead of 1914, the conflict would likely have been shorter, less industrially destructive, and politically transformative in different ways—but still deeply destabilizing.

In 1905 Europe was already tense. The Russo‑Japanese War had just exposed Russian weakness, Germany was challenging France over Morocco, and alliance blocs were solidifying. However, key structural conditions of 1914 were not yet fully in place. Germany’s navy was smaller, Britain’s military coordination with France was less developed, and many of the technological advances that made World War I so lethal—large-scale heavy artillery production, widespread machine-gun deployment, advanced trench systems, poison gas, tanks, long-range submarines—were either immature or not yet integrated into war planning. Mobilization timetables were also less rigid.

A 1905 war might plausibly have started from the First Moroccan Crisis or from instability in the Balkans. The likely sides would still resemble the later blocs: Germany and Austria-Hungary versus France and Russia, with Britain uncertain at first but probably drawn in if Germany violated Belgian neutrality or threatened French collapse. However, Russia in 1905 was militarily and politically weakened by defeat in East Asia and domestic revolution. If war had erupted then, Russia might have struggled even more severely than in 1914–17, potentially collapsing earlier or seeking a quick peace.

Because military technology was slightly less optimized for entrenched stalemate, the war might have been more mobile at the outset. Germany’s Schlieffen-style planning was already forming, but French defenses were less extensive and British expeditionary capacity smaller. A rapid German victory over France was somewhat more plausible in 1905 than in 1914. If France had been defeated quickly, Britain might have faced a stark choice between negotiated peace and prolonged naval war. A shorter continental war ending in German dominance could have reshaped Europe without the prolonged attrition that exhausted all sides in reality.

Austria-Hungary, still relatively more stable in 1905, might have fared better than it did in 1914–18. The Ottoman Empire, though fragile, had not yet suffered the Balkan Wars and might have entered a conflict in a somewhat stronger position. Conversely, Italy’s alignment would have been even more uncertain.

Crucially, the absence of a long, grinding total war would have altered the ideological aftermath. The Russian Revolution might still have occurred—Russia was already unstable—but its trajectory would differ depending on whether defeat was swift or avoided. Without four years of mass slaughter and economic collapse across Europe, the extreme radicalization that fueled Bolshevism and later fascism might have been less intense. A shorter war without catastrophic reparations might not have created the same conditions for Nazism in Germany. On the other hand, if Germany had won decisively and established continental hegemony, resentment in France and Britain could have produced a different kind of long-term rivalry and perhaps a later, more deliberate war.

The United States in 1905 was less globally engaged. Without unrestricted submarine warfare (not yet fully developed) or prolonged stalemate, U.S. intervention would have been less likely. This would reduce the emergence of the U.S. as a decisive global power at that stage.

Overall, a 1905 World War I would probably have been shorter and somewhat less technologically catastrophic, with a greater chance of a decisive continental victory—most plausibly for Germany—rather than the mutual exhaustion that characterized 1914–1918. The long-term result might not have prevented a second great war, but it could have produced a very different twentieth century, with altered timelines for revolution, fascism, American ascendancy, and European decline.

items.question: What If A clash between Rockefeller/Cisneros vs Quayle/Alexander in the US 1996 elections
human_answers: Think about it--when Truman lost, it wasn't *just* because Democrats had been in power a long time. It was *also* because Harry Truman never saw a hornet's nest he didn't want to kick, a temperamental flaw that contributed to a sense of chaos in all walks of life. Combine that with the endemic corruption issues that come from twenty years in power, and you've got a recipe for a one term president. A distinct but similar dynamic appears with the coming of Nixon. Nobody believed LBJ about anything by 1968, and that rubbed off on Humphrey, who was (ironically) more upright but much weaker than Johnson, and the Hump never could shake the Credibility Gap issues he inherited. The loss of trust on all fronts created widespread anger and chaos followed in the wake of that anger. Add to that the endemic corruption issues that come from eight years of Kennedy and Johnson, and you've got a recipe for a Nixon win. No surprise, this is basically the exact same setup that takes down Nixon and Ford. What you might notice here is that the personality flaws of the individual in the White House combine with the problems of institutional corruption that arise after years in power to create a scandal unique to the time and place that ends up consuming everyone involved. I would imagine that a Bush I who gets a second term--by *some* miracle--is going to make some similar mistakes to the ones his son made. They had many of the same advisors, after all. Here, Bush I had none of Bush II's cocksure self assurance to distract from whatever Middle East quagmire he drags the US into, and I think he would crash and burn more quickly in terms of public approval. You might imagine a scenario where Clinton's scandals + much better Perot popular vote= an apparent Bush landslide, where Bush makes the error of mistaking his opponents' divisions for his own strength. I won't get into details because it's current politics, but if you want an example of just such an outcome, look at the results of the last UK general election. The bigger question to me is why America would turn to a plutocrat like Rockefeller after 16 years of "Greed is Good."

Okay, the idea is that this story is loosely based on some ideas from other users who wrote their stories*. The general idea is to create a story with some overall meaning using all of this. So, the story is about how, before the 1988 elections, a recession (like the one in the 90s) occurs. This causes Bush to win by a much smaller margin than OTL (301-236 EVs), resulting in the Democrats gaining more seats in the Senate and the House. This leads to Bush panicking, causing him to try to appease both Reaganite Republicans and more moderate Republicans, although I haven't decided what his cabinet would look like. Anyway, because of this, the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait is delayed until August 18, 1991. Furthermore, Iraq decides to invade the east coast of Saudi Arabia on December 26, 1991, that is, 130 days after the invasion of Kuwait. This leads to larger chain reactions overall, but they are not important at this moment. Two important points should also be added: 1. There were no Yugoslav Wars, therefore Bush was perhaps less concerned about the situation developing in the Balkans and set an earlier deadline (than OTL) for a ceasefire in Iraq, which ended on February 24, 1992. 2. The Iraqi Civil War did not end until 1993, so there was an incentive to be more attentive to the problems of other countries. This resulted in a much more effective Gulf War, and Saddam was overthrown a few days before the coalition reached Baghdad, but these are details. What you're probably wondering is... how did Bush win the 1992 election? Well, it was for several reasons. Like the Gulf War, the fact that the Soviet Union was doing stupid things, that the US was able to recover from the recession thanks to contracts with Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, and most importantly, that each and every one of Bill Clinton's sex scandals was revealed. Ultimately, the election ended in a landslide victory for Bush (343-195 EVs). Bush's second term was relatively fruitful**. In foreign policy, he had some relative successes, such as Somalia, and some major successes, such as Rwanda. The economy was booming, and everything was going well. But people were starting to get tired of 16 years of Republican presidency and a Democratic option that wasn't showing it could win 4 elections in a row. Therefore, the Democratic primaries would be an opportunity to determine who could win the 1996 election once and for all. I have a vague idea of who the Democratic candidates might be in the primaries; they would be: ● Jay Rockefeller – He would be the one to win because of his establishment base and because he represents a remnant of the New Deal era, making him the best candidate. ● Henry Cisneros – The surprise candidate of the primaries, someone no one expected to win so many states, even though he's a senator who won the 1990 midterm Senate elections. I think he would come in second or third. ● Jesse Jackson – I'm sure he would see this as the perfect opportunity to run in the 1996 elections. He would run with the rainbow coalition and say that the reason they didn't win the last election was because Bill Clinton was a moderate white Southerner and, above all, a womanizer. Therefore, I see him coming in second or third, but I highly doubt the establishment would want him as their candidate. ● Bill Bradley – He would be the progressive candidate the establishment would prefer over Jackson, but I doubt he would win many states, to be honest. ● Joe Biden - Same as Bradley, but being liberal, not progressive. ● Kent Conrad - Okay, I'd have to justify myself here. I'm actually basing this on some hypothetical 1996 primaries , and I thought it would be interesting and funny to add him as a wildcard candidate. I think he could win Iowa, but I doubt it. In the end, Jay Rockefeller won the primaries, with Jackson and Cisneros coming very close to victory. The Democratic national nomination process ended with Jay Rockefeller as the presidential candidate, and, as happened in the 1988 nomination, a Texan (Henry Cisneros) was chosen, while the protesting defectors voted for Jesse Jackson. The Republican primaries and nomination process is simpler. All the candidates who ran in the 1996 primaries OTL are running ITTL, the difference being that Dan Quayle runs and wins the primary and the Republican nomination. Lamar Alexander came in second in the primaries and became Quayle's running mate. Now, some details I'd like to add are that a) Jesse Jackson would say a few words that would unify all racial demographics in the Rockefeller/Cisneros formula, and Dan Quayle would say something so stupid/racist against Chicanos that it would be repudiated by all centrists; that would be very funny. And that's all I could think of for this scenario***. *The stories I use as a base are: New World Empire: The Second Term of George H.W. Bush Al Grito de Guerra: the Second Mexican Revolution The Rise and Fall of the Vlasov's Russia: The last years of the Soviet Union without Boris YeltsinThird Time's The Charm: A World Without The Yugoslav Wars Daltonia's Test Thread Exocet - the Effects of a different Falklands Paper Doves in Flight: Poland & The World After Communism **For those who want to know, the cabinet is: President: George Bush Vice President: Dan Quayle Secretary of State: James Baker Secretary of Treasury: Jack Kemp Secretary of Defense: Dick Cheney Attorney General: William Barr Secretary of the Interior: Manuel Lujan Jr Secretary of Agriculture: C. Boyden Gray Secretary of Commerce: Barbara Franklin Secretary of Labor: Bill Brock Secretary of Health and Human Services: C. Everett Koop Secretary of Housing and Urban Development: Andrew Card Secretary of Transportation: Sam Skinner Secretary of Energy: James Watkins Secretary of Education: Lamar Alexander Secretary of Veteran Affairs: Ed Derwinski Director of the Office of Management and Budget: Nicholas Brady Counselor to the President: Clayton Yuetter National Security Advisor: Brent Scowcroft Press Secretary: Marlin Fitzwater ***This took me I don't know how many hours, I was literally at it from 4 am until 8:11 am, I want to die

If the 1996 U.S. presidential election had featured a contest between a Rockefeller/Cisneros ticket and a Quayle/Alexander ticket, the race would likely have centered on competing visions of moderate internationalist Republicanism versus conservative, culturally traditional Republicanism—with significant implications for party alignment and electoral geography.

Assuming “Rockefeller” refers to a moderate, northeastern Republican in the mold of the Rockefeller wing (for example, a figure ideologically similar to Nelson Rockefeller, though by 1996 that tradition was largely diminished), paired with Henry Cisneros, a Hispanic Democrat and former HUD Secretary, the ticket would likely have positioned itself as centrist, business-friendly, socially moderate, and strongly internationalist. Cisneros would have added demographic and regional appeal, especially among Latino voters and in the Sun Belt, while signaling a bipartisan, technocratic approach to governance.

On the other side, a Quayle/Alexander ticket would have combined Dan Quayle’s social conservatism and ties to the Reagan-era Republican base with Lamar Alexander’s gubernatorial and education-policy credentials. This ticket would likely have emphasized traditional family values, smaller government, welfare reform, and cultural conservatism, while also promoting education reform and pragmatic federalism.

The election’s dynamics would depend heavily on the broader political environment. In the real 1996 context—economic expansion, low inflation, and post–Cold War stability—a centrist, pro-business Rockefeller/Cisneros ticket could have had a structural advantage if it successfully appealed to suburban moderates and independents. It might have performed especially well in the Northeast, Upper Midwest, and parts of the West Coast, reclaiming territory that had drifted Democratic in the 1990s.

However, Quayle/Alexander would likely have consolidated the conservative South and much of the interior West, mobilizing evangelical voters and culturally conservative Democrats. The race could have accelerated the ideological sorting of the parties: a Rockefeller-led GOP might have fractured the Republican base, with social conservatives feeling alienated, while a Quayle-led ticket could have deepened the party’s rightward shift.

Electorally, the outcome would hinge on turnout and suburban margins. A moderate Republican ticket might have been competitive in states like California, Illinois, and New Jersey, potentially reshaping the electoral map. Conversely, if conservative turnout surged and moderate Republicans defected or stayed home, Quayle/Alexander could have built a strong Electoral College path through the South, Plains, and competitive Midwestern states like Ohio and Missouri.

In the longer term, a Rockefeller/Cisneros victory might have prolonged the viability of a centrist, coalition-building Republican Party and slowed the ideological polarization of the late 1990s and 2000s. A Quayle/Alexander victory, by contrast, would likely have reinforced the ascendancy of social conservatism within the GOP and accelerated partisan realignment along cultural lines.

Overall, the election would probably have been competitive, but in the mid-1990s economic climate, a centrist, pro-growth Rockefeller/Cisneros ticket might have held a narrow edge—especially if it successfully bridged business Republicans, suburban moderates, and minority voters in key battleground states.
