items.question: What If Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley.
human_answers: No Elvis will have minimal effect. Yes he was a popular Singer but he didn’t write anything. So the songs he is famous for will still exist. Will his lose have effects on music? Obviously. But it is not like music won’t more or less still evolve as it did. The lost of one singer is not going to have that drastic an effect there are simply to many of them. And as such someone else will slot in to become the “it” singer of that time. This is Not Like removing a given general from a given battle. In a battle the general has direct influence on the fighting. Swapping him out with someone else can have drastic effect. Who sings Hound Dog… not so much. Yes the song may or may not do worse at the charts and it may or may not have an impact on a company or a song writers career, But the removal of a singer is not effecting WW2. Singers and actors while obviously famous people in general are a dime a dozen! And pretty replaceable in most circumstances. Yes they have impact but is is hard to quantify. Yeah someone else singing a sang may mean that two people that loved that song and it formed the core of how they hooked up may not get it on in the back of a 1953 Chevy but… how the hell would anyone know that for certain? The impact of actors and singers and other people who are famous because they are famous has little impact if they are changed. You want an example of an impact from no Elvis? My uncle and his friend would not have had weekend gigs playing in the band of an Elvis impersonator. And I would have been able to stay home and avoid going to a really dull county fair that my folks dragged me to. And who knows I may have gotten farther with the pretty blonde next door sooner. But I doubt it. I know we have all heard of Elvis but he was simply not that important. I challenge you to tell me what he actually did that has a significance to history, or music. Yes a lot of folks imitated his style and his look and yes a lot of people bought his music. But if anything he had a negative knock on in music as his manager was an As$#@&*(. Of the first order and screwed many a song writers over big time. So there is a reasonable likelihood that some songwriters may have done better. Now the Beatles are a bit different. They wrote a LOT of music and some of that music had an impact on other writers. Once again the impact of them not being around has a knock on in pop culture in that you don’t get impersonator and it will effect in minor ways various individuals when they have to listen to different singers or whatever. But as with Elvis that has minimal influence on anything. And is almost impossible to document. But the lose of the songs that they wrote will have an effect on the evolution of music much more then not have an inspiration for singers shacking their hips. For example the Beach Boys will be effected as the album Pet Sounds was a direct response to some of the work the Beatles were doing. Writers have a more significant impact on music as they tend to influence each other a lot and it is simpler to replace the person singing any given song then the person that wrote it. Just look at how many people have success doing covers of songs. So the problem with this kind of post is twofold. One it is very very very hard to predict exactly what will change. For example will not having the song Dont Stop (thinking about tomorrow) influence the outcome one of the 1992 presidential election? Probably not. So you are dealing with things that are very nebulous. And if it just a singer that is even hard to say as it is possible that some unknown singer could get a break with the song instead. Elvis didn’t write his music so pretty much all his songs would be song by someone else if he disappeared. And the second problem with this kind of topic on this group is that there are a lot more people that know history and military stuff to a significant degree then know music. At least in the way that it will change. I probably know the words to 75% of the songs sung by Elvis and the Beatles but I don’t know who wrote most of Elvises songs nor who produced any songs for either of them. But I either know or have books that tell me who the major officers where at pretty much any major battle in the Civil War. And I know or can find out enough about most of them to have a good guess how swapping them will effect a given battle. But who can say what guy would have walked through the door and gotten the opportunity to perform if Elvis was gone. Frankly there are thousands of better singers in the world than Elvis that never got the chance. But the combination of his abilities and the opritunities he got made him a superstar. But it is impossible to know who would have gooten that chance if he was not there. But there are only a handful of people that may have been promoted if Montgomery got ran over by a tank.

I’m not saying that nothing would change. There absolutely would be changes from neither artist existing. It’s just that fundamentally: You still have popular music derived from Black American musical traditions. You still have a push away from large swing-style bands and towards smaller guitar-based bands - especially since before the digital era the guitar is the most accessible music instrument for young people wanting to make music. You still have the Baby Boom yielding a much larger youth cohort than before - thus yielding a significant generational divide by the early to mid 1960s as they’ve grown up having not known the struggles of their parents or older siblings - and have more room tackling lifestyle changes without worry for economic precarity. You still have big labels and radio stations wanting to play “different music” for “different races” so to speak. And with that you still have white singers becoming popular for their heavily sanitized covers of black R&B songs ( looks at Pat Boone ). You still have the post-WWII dominance and saturation of American pop culture - including music - in Europe and across the globe. And since the UK and the Commonwealth have virtually zero language barrier with the US - music that imitates American musical traditions (twice removed from Black American roots) has the potential to take off. You still have the advancements in recording technology that gave artists room to make more experimental and groundbreaking music than before. Plus the steady rise of FM radio later in the 1960s to provide a market for more ambitious music. You still have the Sexual Revolution to loosen norms around sex. On top of the various other drivers of the counterculture. You still have the payola scandal and the burnout of 1950s rock stars causing the 1959-64 dearth in the quality of pop music. But that’s just structurally speaking. Aesthetically speaking, things could be shifted around - with some new genre inspired by surf rock and garage rock (though realistically not actually either one of them) blowing up out of nowhere by 1964-65 - and Pat Boone is the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll all the artists of the 1960s are inspired by in terms of singing style and aura. While British rock bands are basically seen as a store brand that only gains later appreciation in the social media era decades later a la Japanese city pop. But it would still fundamentally fit the bigger variables that had been brewing years or even decades before the mid 1960s.

While the absence of the Beatles (and particularly Lennon and McCartney) would deprive us of some very good songs, there were vast numbers of competent bands in Britain that could have filled the niche if given the opportunity- whether together or singly. The bigger impact would probably have been on the penetration of British artists into the USA [1], but that's quite likely to happen eventually because there's money to be made from big crowds of relatively wealthy teenagers who happen to hit on a good enough band. The other impact might have been on the pressure to become singer-songwriters, rather than just singers/performers. Again, money is a big driver so it's likely to happen sooner or later. Otherwise, US innovation is likely to remain largely unchanged (Iggy and the Stooges will still form, and the drivers for hippy culture and rock bands is still there). Meanwhile, the Rolling Stones would still be experimenting with blues and quality musicians like Buddy Holly, Carl Perkins will be filling the niche that Elvis is no longer dominating. In short, different but still broadly recognisable. [1] The Monkees are unlikely to be formed, but songs like Day Dream Believer are too good not to end up being a success, even if it takes a few cover versions to become a real hit.

No Beatles or Elvis? Hmmm the amateur musicologist in me (that's what happens when you're a musician, who has also played in rock bands) says that rock 'n roll would still exist. The chances are also good that you would still have its superstar in the 50s - I read years ago that there were plans to push Carl Perkins (he of "Blue Suede Shoes" fame) towards superstardom by Sun Records. He might have actually become one if he hadn't suffered a major injury (he was in a car crash that kept him out of commission for a long time). Sam Phillips and even Elvis stated that Carl was doing rockabilly before Elvis, and unlike Elvis, Carl was also a songwriter. Most musicians will tell you that having that skill gives you much more staying power - you're not just a performer, you can make money off or songwriting royalties. By the time Carl recovered from the car crash it was too late, Elvis had overshadowed him. Jerry Lee Lewis, courtesy of his flamboyant personality might have become the 50s rock 'n roll superstar (how long he would have lasted would have depended upon whether or not he was still foolish enough to marry his underage cousin). The 60s? Hmmm that's not so certain - in the early 60s, rock 'n roll seemed to be on it's way out (or at least heading towards just being a niche genre of music). What rock 'n roll there was on Top 40 radio was mostly bland, and barely even qualified as rock 'n roll (Frankie Avalon anybody?). The Beach Boys were making songs with lame-o lyrics ("Be True to Your School", etc.). Even in Europe it was only doing so-so - I remember reading an interview of Jimmy Page (who along with playing guitar in Led Zeppelin, and the Yardbirds, was an in-demand session guitarist in the early and mid 60s), where he stated that in the early 60s, it was hard to even find rock 'n roll recording sessions to play on. Without the Beatles, rock'n roll might have just kept on being 50s-style teen hearthrob music performed by Cliff Richard, instrumental music played by bands like The Shadows (who also happened to be Cliff Richard's backing band), and possibly music played by 50s American rock 'n roll musicians, who were going nowhere in the USA with their careers (Bo Diddly, Eddie Cochran, etc. performed extensively in Europe in the early 60s when their careers fizzled out in the US). One of the big elements of the Beatles that helped to propel them to stardom IMO, was that for its time (the early 60s), the Beatles' music was considered HARD ROCK. As a result, it had more energy to it than your typical music of the period, and people liked it. The Stones? They were in their infancy, playing what is to me, watered down blues, that sounded nowhere near as intense. That hard rock edge the Beatles had is what kick started rock 'n roll again, and resulted in a million bands wanting to sound like them (even in the US, after they were on the Ed Sullivan Show). No Beatles and IMO, rock 'n roll continues its decline into a niche music genre, with the occasional Top 40 hit by bland groups like Gary Pucket and The Union Gap, Gary Lewis and The Playboys, etc. Not much in the way of edgy, interesting music. In the US, Link Wray never charts as high as he did with "Rumble" (which was actually banned by radio stations because it was "too threatening - it'll incite people to riot"), and Lonnie Mack at most has a few very modest hits like he had with "Wham".

Oh, for the love of Pete, not THIS again.... I just don't understand how some on this board can analyze military events down to the level of minutiae where they can argue that if a particular German general farted at a given moment in 1940, the entirety of World War II would come out differently, and yet at the same time assume that popular culture would remain essentially unaltered without the presence of two of its most important figures. Just as one example: before the Beatles, there was no such thing as a "British rock and roll group" in the eyes of Americans, and particularly American record companies, radio programmers, and concert promoters. Cliff Richard, who was Britain's biggest rock and roll superstar prior to the Beatles, went absolutely nowhere in America. Americans knew that rock and roll had originated in the U.S., and they were very parochial about it - the assumption, and it was not often wrong, before the Beatles was that anything coming from Britain would be a poor copy of records American teenagers already owned. (And it WAS teenagers almost exclusively who listened to rock and roll in 1963; projecting one's own current cultural dynamics into the past is part of the reason one gets lost). No British rock group - not one - had broken in the U.S. before 1964. The Beatles themselves at first were turned down by Capitol, the American division of EMI, who held their recording contract in the UK; Capitol refused to issue their first four singles in the U.S. It took the "Beatlemania" phenomenon to convince Capitol that it was worth giving the Beatles a shot, which enabled Beatlemania to cross the Atlantic. I'm sorry, but it's not as if "Holliemania" or "Dave Clark Fivemania" simply takes the place of that. There's a whole set of intangibles here. You can't just assume that you like the Rolling Stones better, so they automatically take the place of the Beatles. It would never have worked like that. What happens to the Rolling Stones becomes essentially undefinable. And that's just one example. I didn't even address the fact of no Elvis - which probably would have meant no Beatles AND virtually none of the other British Invasion acts either. Removing Elvis from the picture (which automatically would remove the Beatles as we know them) changes the ENTIRE trajectory of popular music from that day to this, in well-nigh unpredictable ways. Period.
items.original_question: What if Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley. American Singer and Actor Elvis Presley and British Rock Band The Beatles are the most Influential musicians in existence. With the former codifying Rockabilly and is credited for advancing the Feminist movement in America, and the Latter spearheaded the British Invasion, increased public interest in Psychedelic Drugs, Asian Spirituality and heralded the Album Era. Let's say both the musician and the Band never had any interest in music, preventing the codifying of Rockabilly and The British Invasion. How would this influence modern music?

items.model_answer:
If modern music had developed without Elvis Presley and The Beatles, it would likely still have evolved into a global, commercially dominant force—but its sound, speed of change, and cultural impact would have been markedly different.

Elvis Presley was pivotal in bringing rhythm and blues, gospel, and country together into a mainstream-friendly form of rock and roll in the 1950s. Without him, rock and roll would still have existed—artists like Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Sister Rosetta Tharpe, and Fats Domino were already shaping it—but it may not have crossed over into white, middle-class America as rapidly or as explosively. The racial integration of popular music might have proceeded more slowly, and the music industry may have remained more segmented by race and region for a longer time. The image of the rebellious, sexually charged youth idol might also have taken a different form or emerged later, potentially delaying the cultural centrality of the teenage market.

Without The Beatles, the 1960s would have been even more dramatically altered. The Beatles did not just produce hit songs; they transformed expectations about songwriting, studio experimentation, album structure, and the role of the band as a self-contained creative unit. The “British Invasion” might not have happened in the same way, which would have changed the trajectory of bands like The Rolling Stones, The Who, and countless others who benefited from the transatlantic breakthrough. The shift from singles to albums as cohesive artistic statements might have been slower. Studio innovation—multitracking, concept albums, genre blending—would still have emerged, but perhaps less quickly or under different leadership, possibly from American soul, psychedelic, or folk artists instead.

Culturally, both Elvis and The Beatles served as symbols of generational change. Without Elvis, the 1950s youth rebellion might have lacked a single, electrifying figure. Without The Beatles, the 1960s counterculture might have had a less unified soundtrack. Music would still have intersected with civil rights, antiwar activism, and social transformation, but the emotional and symbolic cohesion provided by these artists would have been diffused across many performers rather than concentrated in a few iconic figures.

Technologically and economically, the industry would likely have matured more gradually. The Beatles’ experimentation accelerated the idea of the recording studio as an instrument, influencing progressive rock, art rock, and eventually electronic and experimental genres. Without that push, popular music might have stayed more performance-oriented and less studio-driven for longer. Similarly, Elvis’s mass appeal demonstrated the immense profitability of youth culture, helping solidify the modern pop star system.

items.question: What If the Royal Navy had deployed carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward?
human_answers: Far too big Even with folding wings I don't think they would fit on the elevators and would take up too much room in the hanger even of they fit which again I suspect not Its landing on performance of he Beaufighter is about the same as an avenger (60 knots?) but its much heavier than the TBF so I am not sure the arrestor cables of the day could handle such a plane. Its a nice idea but its too much of a plane for the carriers of the day - might work on an Audacious class but not the carriers built in the late 30s. The Whispering Death is already doing sterling work as a land based anti shipping aircraft during the war and it has great range - not quite 'Rikko' (G3m and G4m Japanese bombers) range, but close too it, but still a scourge where ever it operated.

In the last thread on the subject I mentioned, given any wing-break would have to be somewhat outboard the engines*, that you could probably take one up and down on Implacable's forward lift but the hangar height would preclude you rolling it off. You could store one in Illustrious's hangar, if you made it from a kit of parts, as the lift is too narrow. So deck parks only. You could use some form of depressing oleos to lower the Beaufighter's resting angle. You might just scrape it into Implacable's hangar but clearances would be marginal. Any kind of seaway would make deck handling tricky to impossible. You could also only load a torpedo on the flight deck with the aircraft back up to full height. I also suggested an increased-chord rudder and handed props because the Beaufighter could be a handful with all the room in the world. Operating a Beau on/off of a carrier is an expensive way to give a pilot a coronary... ETA: The wing-breaks are going to be in the order of 25ft apart and Illustrious's elevators are only 22ft across. Folding the wings is also going to involve re-siting the cooling ducts from the outboard leading edge.

items.model_answer:
If the Royal Navy had fielded effective carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward, the immediate impact would have been a significant strengthening of Fleet Air Arm strike power at a time when it was comparatively weak. In 1940–41, British carriers relied largely on the Fairey Swordfish and later the Albacore—slow, biplane torpedo bombers that were vulnerable in contested airspace. A navalized Beaufort (torpedo bomber) and Beaufighter (long-range strike fighter) would have provided faster, more heavily armed, and more survivable options years earlier than the Barracuda and Firebrand eventually did.

In the Mediterranean, this could have been especially consequential. During operations against the Italian fleet and Axis convoys to North Africa, faster torpedo bombers with better defensive armament would have improved strike survivability against fighters and flak. Sea Beaufighters, with their heavy cannon armament, could have served as powerful convoy-escort and anti-shipping strike aircraft, potentially increasing Axis shipping losses earlier and reducing pressure on Malta. Carrier task forces might have operated more aggressively, with better organic air cover and strike reach.

In the Atlantic, carrier-based Beaufighters could have enhanced anti-shipping and anti-submarine sweeps, particularly against surface raiders and long-range reconnaissance aircraft such as the Fw 200 Condor. Their speed and firepower would have made them formidable convoy defenders from escort carriers, potentially closing the mid-Atlantic air gap sooner or at least more effectively before long-range land-based aircraft became widespread.

In the Far East, the presence of more capable strike aircraft on British carriers in 1941–42 might have marginally improved British naval air power against Japan. However, without adequate fighter cover comparable to Japanese Zeroes, and given broader strategic weaknesses, this alone would not have reversed defeats such as the loss of Force Z or the fall of Singapore. The main limitation would still have been numbers, training, radar integration, and carrier doctrine rather than aircraft performance alone.

There would also have been trade-offs. Both the Beaufort and Beaufighter were relatively large, heavy aircraft. Operating them from British carriers—many of which were armored-deck ships with smaller hangars—would have reduced aircraft complements. Deck handling and structural modifications would have been challenging, potentially limiting sortie rates. The Royal Navy might have fielded fewer but more capable aircraft per carrier, changing operational patterns but not necessarily multiplying overall striking power.

Overall, early deployment of Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters would likely have strengthened British naval strike capability in 1940–42, improved anti-shipping effectiveness in the Mediterranean and Atlantic, and reduced aircraft losses in some operations. However, it would not by itself have transformed the strategic balance of the war at sea. Industrial constraints, pilot training, radar coordination, carrier numbers, and broader Allied resource limitations would still have defined the scale and timing of British naval recovery.

items.question: What If : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944
human_answers: The only Southerner who got any serious support at the DNC in 1944 was Alabama Senator John H. Bankhead II, who came in a distant third with 98 votes (8.33%) on the first ballot. The only other (non Alben W. Barkley) Southerners who got even one vote were: J. Melville Broughton (Governor of North Carolina), Prentice Cooper (Governor of Tennessee), Robert S. Kerr (Senator from Oklahoma), Herbert O'Conor (Governor of Maryland), Claude Pepper (Senator from Florida), Sam Rayburn (Speaker of the House), and Bascom N. Timmons (D.C. based newspaperman who grew up in Texas). Of these, only Bankhead II, Barkley, Broughton, Cooper, Kerr, and O’Conor got double digits. So your best case scenario is Roosevelt and/or the convention see a need to nominate a Southerner, and go with Bankhead II who IOTL died on June 12, 1946 following a stroke on May 24, 1946, which means you end up with three Presidents in little over a year. Based on the 1886 Succession Act, Bankhead II’s successor would be none other than… James F. Byrnes. IOTL, Truman appointed him in July of 1945, and it’s pretty likely Bankhead II does similarly, wanting to support a follow Southerner. (Prior to the Succession Act of 1947, neither the Speaker of the House nor the President pro tempore of the Senate were in the line of succession.) So in a roundabout way, you do end up with Byrnes as President…

Right. Byrnes thought he was Roosevelt's choice. Truman went to the DNC planning to make a nominating speech for Byrnes. If Byrnes does get the nod... FDR wins in 1944 anyway. But things diverge after that. IMO the Republicans sweep in 1946 as OTL. Byrnes was a very capable man and won't make any big missteps, so IMO he will be renominated in 1948. There may be a feeling that the 1948 nomination is a poisoned chalice, what with the 1946 GOP sweep and general public fatigue with 16 years of Democrat Presidents. The "Humphreyite" liberals may still try to push a civil rights plank at the DNC, but against Byrnes' at least tacit opposition will fail. They won't bolt to support Wallace overtly. Instead they may sit back to watch Byrnes crash and burn in November, while they regroup for 1952. Byrnes will lose a fair number of voters to Wallace outside the South. Also, AIUI, Dewey chose to soft-pedal civil rights OTL in the vain hope of winning some Upper South states with the Democrats divided. TTL that ignis fatuus isn't around, so Dewey probably emphasizes civil rights to draw the increasingly important black vote in the North and also some white liberals. This should be enough for Dewey to win. The next question is whether he has enough "coat tails" for Republicans to hold Congress. Another question is how the civil rights issue shapes across the next decade. OTL, leadership on the issue was taken by liberal non-Southern Democrats, with the low-key support of Republicans. The first cracks in the "Solid South" came in the 1950s, as a few white Southerners who could no longer rely on the national Democratic party to protect Jim Crow found they could vote Republican. If under Dewey, Republicans claim the leading role, that's not going to happen. The "Humphreyites" will gain control of the Democrats by 1952; there may be a Dixiecrat ticket that year. Dewey will be re-elected, barring some debacle in Korea or whatever. Warren won't be Chief Justice, but the Court will still be making rulings like Brown .

If Franklin D. Roosevelt had chosen a segregationist vice‑presidential running mate in 1944 instead of Harry S. Truman, the consequences would likely have been significant, especially because the vice president ultimately succeeded him. Since FDR died in April 1945, any running mate in 1944 was effectively a president‑in‑waiting. The key question, then, is how a segregationist president in 1945–49 would have altered civil rights, party politics, and early Cold War dynamics.

First, civil rights policy would almost certainly have stalled or regressed. Truman, though a product of Missouri machine politics, surprised many by endorsing civil rights, desegregating the armed forces in 1948, and advocating federal anti‑lynching and anti‑poll tax measures. A committed Southern segregationist president would not have done this. The armed forces might have remained segregated through the Korean War. Federal civil rights enforcement would likely have been weaker, and symbolic federal support for Black veterans and civil rights activists would have been diminished at a crucial postwar moment. This would not have stopped the long-term civil rights movement, but it might have delayed key federal actions and altered the timeline of desegregation in the military and possibly in federal employment.

Second, the Democratic Party’s internal fracture might have played out differently. In 1948, Southern Democrats bolted the party over Truman’s civil rights platform, forming the Dixiecrat movement. If the president himself had been a segregationist Southerner, that split might not have occurred in the same way. Instead, Northern liberals and Black voters might have become more alienated. The New Deal coalition—an uneasy alliance of Southern whites, Northern urban workers, and Black voters—could have cracked from the other direction. Black voters, who had been moving toward the Democratic Party since the New Deal, might have reconsidered their alignment earlier, potentially reshaping urban politics in the late 1940s.

Third, foreign policy might have been less affected than domestic civil rights, but not entirely unchanged. The early Cold War consensus—containment, the Marshall Plan, NATO—depended more on broader institutional and elite agreement than on Truman personally. However, Truman’s framing of the Cold War included rhetorical commitments to democracy and freedom that increasingly clashed with segregation at home. A segregationist president would have faced sharper international criticism, especially as the United States positioned itself as leader of the “free world.” Soviet propaganda regularly highlighted American racial injustice; a president openly committed to segregation could have intensified that vulnerability, potentially complicating U.S. diplomacy in decolonizing regions of Asia and Africa.

Finally, the symbolic dimension matters. Truman’s presidency marked an early moment when the federal executive branch tentatively sided with civil rights claims. Even if Congress blocked much of his agenda, the executive order desegregating the military set a precedent for later federal action. Without that precedent, later Democratic administrations—Kennedy and Johnson—might have faced a different institutional and political landscape. The civil rights realignment of the 1960s might still have happened, but possibly with different timing and partisan configurations.

In sum, if FDR had selected a segregationist vice president in 1944, the most immediate and lasting impact would likely have been a delay in federal civil rights initiatives and a different trajectory for party realignment. The broader structure of postwar American power and Cold War policy would probably have remained intact, but the moral and political positioning of the United States at home and abroad would have been more openly compromised at a formative moment.

items.question: What If the Allies lose on the Salonica front?
human_answers: Alan Wakefield (IWM expert on Salonika, among other subjects) commented that most of the Bulgarian forces in September 1918 facing the British were well motivated, apart from the 1st Macedonian Bde that consisted of many men of Serbian origin. It was the collapse further west when the French & Serbian forces broke through three lines of defence, followed by the Greek breakthrough at Petit Couronne and Doiran Hill to the Bulgarian second line that unhinged the Bulgarian defences. Bulgarian C-in-C Todorov met with the German commanders von Steuben (German 11th Army) and von Reuter (Division Reuter) on 18 September, and agreed that Bulgarian 1st Army would be pulled back from positions east of the Vadar River, while the German 11th Army and Bulgarian 3rd Division would maintain contact. However the orders to 1st Army came as a severe blow to morale as the men were celebrating their stalling the British attacks, They started marching to Kosturino Pass but there was a serious shortage of draught animals, and of the survivors: " The majority of horses & oxen were absolutely unfit for work and they had need of at least six months rest in the interior, where they could be well nourished, Others had need of at least 45 days rest" - Major Nedeff, 9th Division, quoted in Under the Devil's Eye (Alan Wakefield & Simon Moody) from which much of the first three paragraphs are sourced. This was when the RAF caught the Bulgarian withdrawal through the passes, causing serious casualties & further delays. With foreign troops now on Bulgarian soil, political opposition to the war in the Sobranie was widespread. The PM, Malinov, was pro-western and had been appointed that June by Tsar Ferdinand with the purpose of proposing an armistice to the Allies, and on 26 September emissaries were sent through the lines to start discussions, although Franchet d'Esperey would only accept an unilateral unconditional armistice, which the Bugarian government then agreed to give, So it looks like the Bulgarian army was in generally good morale status until the final victories sparked by the French, Serbian & Greek forces, when the order of and losses taken on the retreat caused a final decline. But it looks like the home front collapsed first, if the Tsar was considering an armistice in June, so not sure what caused the domestic problems that drove the government to seek peace (I understand that a military rebelliion / mutiny at Radomir formulated by Bulgarian Agrarian National Union attempted to overthrow the government and establish a republic). Wiki suggests the following reasons: - Extreme war weariness, given Bulgaria had been at war since 1912 (short break 1914-15). Exhausted manpower (see #1 above) - I would add this resulted in dissatisfied minority groups supplying more troops, such as Macedonian Serbs & Greeks, diluting the Bulgar core. Both military & civilians suffering extreme food shortages (result of your point regarding harvests?). Troops poorly supplied - not only food but ammunition, clothing, boots, etc. Troops believing profiteers making hay at home at their expense. Feeling of betrayal by their allies, principally Germany, especialy regarding promised levels of supplies not being met, and lack of support for Bulgarian territorial ambitions at expense of Romania. Not sure how far the German troop levels had been reduced as you comment. The impact of the Russian Revolution. The impact of Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (maybe a surrender would't be as bad as keep fighting) Recommended is 'The Enemy is Behind Us': The Morale Crisis in the Bulgarian Army during the Summer of 1918 - Richard C Hall, War in History Vol. 11 No. 4 which again refers to the collapse in morale starting by June 1918. Bulgarian C-in-C Nikola Zhekov reported to Tsar Ferdinand on 121 June that: "Today it is impossible ton have any illusions that the spirit of the soldiers is the same as at the beginning of the war, or even last year." I can't access as I don't have a school account! It does look like some units, such as the 9th (Pleven) Division, kept their high morale almost to the end. My main comment on demoralised forces would apply further north and primarily to the Austro-Hungarian troops who fell apart in October 1918, when I daresay no one suggests they were of high morale status. Earlier in the war that would not be the case, and I reckon me & a mountain goat could hold the Neretva Valley!

When you mentioned the Allies, I almost thought it was World War II. In reality, due to the division of Greece, neither the Entente nor the Central Powers could make any progress on the Thessaloniki front. Launching a large-scale offensive meant turning Greece into a battlefield, alienating more Greeks, and pushing more Greeks to the other side. The Entente was able to launch its offensive on the Macedonian front in 1917-1918 because the Entente countries had a large surplus of French reserves, willing to do everything except attack the Germans, such as conducting political work with the Greeks (Germany's reserves were smaller but more elite, and needed to do more important things; Bulgaria and the Ottomans were absolutely unacceptable to the Greeks). Ultimately, the deployment of hundreds of thousands of soldiers from the core countries of the Triple Entente only resulted in the defeat of one vassal state. The Central Powers could not accept this waste of reserves (unless Italy joined the Central Powers, providing some low ability soldiers). Even so, the problem of resource shortages must be taken into account.

It's my impression that it's something of a convention on this post 1900 forum to use "Entente" instead of "Allies", presumably to avoid confusion with the Allies of WW2. IMVHO I do prefer "Allies" for the WW1 military coalition because "Entente" is a derivation of the "Triple Entente" which applies to France/Russia/Britain, but by the end of WW1 the key great powers were Britain/France/Italy/America (and Russia was out) and there were multiple smaller allied powers. Why couldn't the Central Powers advance? Like, I thought Gallipoli ultimately failed because it was a trench-warfare stalemate; the Allies couldn't overcome a German client state. IIRC the proximal reason for the Gallipoli evacuation was that Bulgaria had joined the Central Powers, providing a route for German war material (not merely advisor personnel) like heavy siege artillery to be delivered to Turkey, which the Allies thought would be decisive. Was that assessment correct? Are you saying the Ottomans (with German support) could do something (push an Allied army into the sea) the Bulgarians (with their German support) could not? Or do you think that if the Allies had dug in on the Gallipoli peninsula in 1916, they might have obtained a stalemate which lasted until 1917/1918 when further offensives could be launched? I read that because of the potential futility of the front, Britain (and France) contemplated withdrawing their troops from mainland Greece before lines were solidified. Surely the Central Powers could have conquered Greece under those circumstances, no? I suppose in a grand strategy sense I recognize Germany was trying to fight a multi-front conflict against [the entire rest of the world] and was ultimately all but certain to lose the war. But in the narrower sense of "could the Balkan theater have played out differently", isn't it possible that the Central Powers could have achieved more success? Like, what if some resources from a different offensive (which surely would see less success than in OTL) devoted towards breaking through on the Macedonian front?

The allies couldn't overcome a German ally with more than 50 divisions and more than a million men on the field you mean, which in 1915 were about as well armed as their own troops. This is not 1942 in the Eastern front. But to get to the actual question in the fall of 1915 Greece was fully mobilized with 16 divisions and 325,000 troops in Macedonia and the Germans were doing their level best to keep Constantine in control and Greece out of the war. If they invade Greek territory you can kiss that neutrality goodbye and these 16 divisions just come into play added to the British and French divisions already landed in Salonica. And you'd better time it after the Serbs have been pushed into retreating into Albania, if your invasion comes before you just saved the lives of a couple hundred thousand Serbs. No. You essentially suggest Berlin says "to hell with the shenanigans to keep the Greeks neutral, let's invade them too. " So you just about gave numerical parity to the defenders... who don't have to move everything but food and fodder for the Macedonian and Turkish fronts though a single track railway going all the way back to Vienna. Before Dobro Polie and Desperate Frankie advancing all the way to Hungary and Austria putting the final nail in the Austro-Hungarian empire's coffin the actual front looked a pretty good deal to Berlin. Over 400,000 allied troops before the Greeks joined, that could be fighting elsewhere contained through mostly Bulgarian manpower... which could not be used elsewhere. Biggest POW camp in the world jokes and all that.

Well, Alternate History Challenge: An equivalent of Dobro Polie and subsequent desperate Frankie advances happen six months to a year earlier than OTL, *before* the Germans start getting pushed back on the western front, not after, and perhaps as a consequence, we get to see see the desperate Frankie international force *keep advancing* through the territory of capitulated Austria-Hungary, and over onto German territory from its southern and eastern borders (to Munich, Passau, Dresden, Gorlitz, Liegnitz or further to Cottbus or Berlin) before the Germans actually capitulate. Could this have ever happened in the right combination of circumstances? Could an earlier resolution of the Greek political divide in favor of the Venizelist side, committing the full Greek Army to the Entente side earlier, have helped with this? What might it take, faster French seduction? Or, going the opposite direction, more in line with what the OP wants, is there any way the Venizelist side could have been so marginalized that the Royalist side in Greece became willing to openly side with the Central Powers and openly welcomed/sought CP support in expelling Allied forces from Salonica and any other parts of Greece at any point during the war?
items.original_question: What if the Allies lose on the Salonica front? As I loosely understand it, the Salonica front was established after the Serbian army was routed. What if the Central Powers were able to continue advancing into Greece and expelled the Allies from the mainland Balkans? The Salonica front in some ways seems to resemble Gallipoli (an Allied lodgment supplied by sea) and the Central powers were able to prevail at Gallipoli, so it seems possible. The Allies also had to deal with the fact that the Greek government was divided - if the Central powers were more successful it seems possible Greece would have “switched sides”, or at least had a compliant government installed.

items.model_answer:
If the Allies had lost decisively on the Salonica (Macedonian) front in World War I, the political and strategic consequences would likely have been significant, especially in the Balkans, though not necessarily decisive for the entire war.

The Salonica front tied down large numbers of Bulgarian, Austro-Hungarian, German, French, British, Serbian, and later Greek troops. If the Central Powers—primarily Bulgaria, backed by Germany and Austria-Hungary—had defeated the Allied Army of the Orient and forced it out of Greece, several immediate effects would follow. Serbia would remain fully occupied, with no chance of liberation in 1918. Bulgaria would secure its territorial gains in Macedonia and strengthen its regional dominance. Greece, which joined the Allies in 1917 after internal political turmoil, might face political collapse or even be forced back into neutrality or a pro-Central Powers alignment.

Strategically, a Central Powers victory in the Balkans would secure their southern flank. It would guarantee uninterrupted land communications from Germany through Austria-Hungary and Bulgaria to the Ottoman Empire. This would ease pressure on the Ottomans by improving supply lines and possibly allow greater coordination in the Middle East. The Central Powers might redeploy some troops from the Balkans to other fronts, particularly Italy or the Western Front.

However, the broader outcome of the war would still hinge on the Western Front and, by 1917–1918, American involvement. Even with a victory at Salonica, Germany would still face the immense industrial and manpower advantage of the United States, Britain, and France. The decisive blows of 1918 historically came from the Allied Hundred Days Offensive in France and the collapse of Bulgaria after the Allied breakthrough at Dobro Pole. If the Allies had instead been defeated in Macedonia, Bulgaria would not have capitulated in September 1918, removing one of the triggers for the cascading collapse of the Central Powers. Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire might have held out longer, and Germany could have avoided the psychological shock of its allies collapsing.

In that sense, an Allied defeat at Salonica might not guarantee a Central Powers victory, but it could prolong the war, stiffen Central Powers morale, and possibly lead to a negotiated peace rather than outright defeat—especially if it coincided with greater German success in the West. The Balkans would likely emerge more firmly under Bulgarian and Austro-Hungarian influence, with Serbia weakened or partitioned, and Greek politics deeply destabilized.

Overall, losing the Salonica front would not automatically hand the Central Powers victory in World War I, but it would remove a key pressure point that historically accelerated their collapse and might significantly alter the timing and terms of the war’s end.

items.question: What If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine?
human_answers: 1 - as noted by the fellow member, the P-40F and L used the Merlin 2 - it was a pretty simple upgrade 3 - engine itself does not require a laminar flow wing; a laminar flow wing will cut some drag, however, and thus allow for some speed increase 4 - historically, it offered some 30 mph over the P-40E at 18000 ft and above, IOW it was an improvement the P-40 badly needed 5 - P-51s used the better Merlins, these with 2-stage supercharger; a P-40 with such an engine would've probably be as fast as the Spitfire IX, but not as fast as the Merlin Mustang, nor as rangy - and thus the answer is 'no' 6 - as-is, the performance was better on the P-40F than on the ubiquitous P-40E; with 2-stage Merlin, it would've probably been good for 400+ mph, and much better rate of climb (the XP-40Q did 420+ mph with a 2-stage supercharged V-1710)

I'll have to take your word for it as I'm forbidden from your links but that sounds about right. A more advanced Merlin won't really help the P-40 though. There are availability issues with the Merlin, as ever, which historically forced Curtiss to revert to the V-1710-81 for the P-40M, despite more than half the production run going to the RAF. Not even every P-40F/L received a Merlin as some were completed as V-1710-81 engined P-40Rs. More though, there is the tale of the XP-60, which was a P-40D fuselage with a new laminar-flow wing. It was an improvement, with 387mph at 22,000ft. Modified as the XP-60D with an enlarged tail, it may or may not have received the V-1650-3 slated for it by the time of it's destruction in a crash on 6th May 1943. It certainly didn't perform any substantive testing with it. By that time the Merlin Mustang was established as superior in performance and was already entering production. The XP-60A with 1425hp V-1710-75, good for 420mph at 29,000ft, was part-cancelled in January 1942 (with the remainder following in June 1943) in favour of P-40Ks, Ls and P-47Gs. I think that is going to be the fate of any advanced or improved P-40 variant. Cancelled in favour of sustained production of known quantities.

If the Curtiss P‑40 had been designed from the outset around the Rolls‑Royce Merlin rather than the Allison V‑1710, it would likely have been a significantly more competitive fighter throughout much of World War II, especially at medium and high altitudes.

The core limitation of early P‑40 variants was not their airframe but their engine installation. The Allison engine used in most P‑40s lacked an effective two‑stage supercharger, which severely limited high‑altitude performance. As a result, P‑40s performed reasonably well at low and medium altitudes—such as in North Africa and China—but struggled against high‑flying German fighters like the Bf 109F and later models. The Merlin, with its superior supercharging system, provided much better high‑altitude power and overall performance, as demonstrated by the transformation of the P‑51 Mustang when it switched from Allison to Merlin power.

In fact, a Merlin‑powered P‑40 did exist: the P‑40F and L variants used Packard‑built Merlin engines. These versions showed improved high‑altitude performance and better climb rates compared to their Allison-powered counterparts. However, they were constrained by an airframe originally designed around a different engine, and they appeared at a time when more advanced fighters were already emerging. If the P‑40 had been designed from the beginning to accommodate the Merlin—with optimized weight distribution, cooling systems, and aerodynamics—it could have achieved better balance, potentially higher top speeds, and improved climb and ceiling earlier in the war.

Such a design might have narrowed the performance gap with contemporary European fighters in 1941–42 and reduced the urgent need to transition to newer types as quickly. However, it is unlikely that even a Merlin-optimized P‑40 would have matched the ultimate performance of later-generation designs like the P‑51D, Spitfire Mk IX, or Fw 190, because the P‑40’s basic airframe had higher drag and less growth potential than those newer fighters.

Strategically, widespread early Merlin use in the P‑40 could also have affected British and American engine allocation. Early in the war, Merlin production was stretched thin, and prioritizing P‑40s might have reduced availability for Spitfires or later Mustangs. Thus, while a Merlin-designed P‑40 would probably have been a more capable and longer‑lived fighter, its overall impact would have depended heavily on production trade‑offs and broader industrial strategy.

In short, a Merlin-designed P‑40 would likely have been a stronger, more competitive fighter in the early and middle years of the war, but it would not have fundamentally altered the trajectory of fighter development or the eventual dominance of more advanced designs.

items.question: PT-109: What If JFK Died on 7/2/43?
human_answers: It seems plausible to me that if Jack were to die in the Pacific, Sr would use connections to ensure that Jr would come home in one piece so that grooming for public office could begin. That said, I've read several accounts that suggest/indicate Jr was not as approachable/astute/able to think on his feet as well as Jack. That might make a political career more challenging: still feasible, but more challenging and quite possibly more costly (Sr might have had to write more and/or larger checks to make things happen?). I could see Jr with a House, and later a Senate seat. Then the question becomes: could he work his way into such a position that Adlai Stevenson might consider him as a running mate in 1956? Arguably, that propelled Jack into the limelight enough to become a presidential contender in 1960. My sense is that Jr would not get the same consideration ITTL that Jack did IOTL. Rather, he would plausibly have tried a presidential run having something like 8-10 years of Senate experience under his belt in 1960. We're talking a crowded field for the Dems in 1960: Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Jr, and the usual cast of favorite sons. Johnson might be the favorite, but not a prohibitive favorite: coming from Texas would assure that. Too manybut Lodge won northerners would be skeptical. On the other hand, Humphrey would definitely not play well in the south. Could Jr emerge as a compromise candidate? Maybe, but he'd be a tough sell in the south given his Catholic faith. My sense is that a protracted, multiple ballot convention would ultimately result in a Johnson nomination, with a middle of the road midwesterner (I'll yield to someone else here) as a VP candidate. Nixon will still be the GOP nominee, but Lodge won't be his running mate: don't need to counter a Kennedy. I suggest it would be MD governor Theodore McKeldin, a man who knew how to work with both sides (he was the last GOP mayor of Baltimore). McKeldin would bring a great deal more to the ticket than Lodge, but that's a pretty low bar. While we're at it, look for the 1960 campaign to be nasty. Lyndon Johnson had few scruples if any as far as that went, so I wouldn't be surprised if he started it. Then all Nixon has to do is take the high road and point out how well things have gone during Ike's tenure, and pump up his role (maybe this time Ike wouldn't make his famous "...if you give me a week..." remark?). And I don't see Richard Daley doing much to help Lyndon Johnson in Chicago, so IL might well flip to the GOP. Long story short: Nixon wins in '60. That leaves 1968 as Jr's next shot at the White House: he wouldn't try to unseat Nixon unless something totally unforeseen happened.

I once posted on another thread about a different pathway that Joe Jr's career would look like. IOTL JFK had the choice of running for Congress or for Lt. Governor of Massachusetts, and he chose to run for Congress in 1946. My alternate path for Joe Jr. had him running for Lt. Governor in 1946 and getting Statewide exposure, IOTL the Democratic ticket lost, but with Joe Sr's money the Democrats win. Joe Jr. runs for US Senate against Republican incumbent Leverett Saltonstall in 1948 and wins in a Democratic year. The main character flaw of Joe Jr. was his fierce loyalty to his father. There is a story about how Joe Sr. was on the Harvard baseball team and by playing on the Harvard-Yale game he would get a letter, but due to anti-Catholic bigotry, he was left on the bench and didn't get a letter. When Joe Jr. as a senior on the team, he was the first baseman and made the final put out of the Harvard-Yale game, and by tradition the ball is given to the team captain and Joe Jr. kept it himself and gave the ball to his father. How this would play out is uncertain, how far would he go in defending Joe Sr.'s isolation? JFK was able use his service to separate himself against any criticism against his father, but could Joe Jr. do that?

Both are possible, but I do think that Jor Sr trying to pull some strings would be more plausible (at least to me). But if Joe Jr still does his mission (maybe the dates between Jack's death and Joe's mission are too close), it could be that Robert gets chosen as the next. That being said... This was something I didn't think about, but from what I read it would make sense. Robert was always known as the black sheep of the family. If Ted was chosen by Joe Sr, he may very well have been thrown into Korea. The only question would be where Ted's future would go: He would have been far too young to run for President in 1960, but he could have won a seat as Senator in Massachusetts (although it would have been difficult). After PT-109 exploded, JFK was able to survive, swimming from the wreck to a nearby island to stay alive while also saving his fellow soldiers. The moment cemented Jack as a war hero, and after his brother Joe died in a special mission, Jack was seen as next in line to join the Senate, before finally becoming President (which we all know how it ended). But what if things went slightly differently? Maybe Jack is closer to the blast and dies in the initial explosion. What next? What would happen to Joe Jr, and by extension, the Kennedy family? In our timeline, Joe Jr was killed in a special mission, but could the death of JFK stopped Joe Jr from going on the mission, and continue to stay alive to be the frontrunner of the family? Joe Jr had approved of Hitler, but his ideals could have easily morphed over time. Could Joe have done what Jack did and become President, and how would his presidency have looked? And if Joe Jr did in fact die anyway, who would replace him? Robert would have been far too young, along with Ted. Would the Kennedy family fade out of the limelight? What would become of the 1960 elections? The more obvious question, with Jack dead, who would be the man to lead the Democrats against Nixon? The most likely options are Hubert Humphrey, Lyndon Baines Johnson, and (although less likely), Adali Stevenson. Who would have been able to win the primaries, and could they have dealt with Nixon? With whoever becomes President, how would their Presidency look, and what could happen to them if they were also assassinated? For me personally, the most likely ticket would have been Johnson, causing him to be President.

If John F. Kennedy had died on July 2, 1943, when PT‑109 was cut in half by the Japanese destroyer *Amagiri*, the immediate impact would have been limited to his family, crew, and wartime morale—but the long-term political consequences for the United States would likely have been substantial.

In 1943 Kennedy was a 26‑year‑old naval officer from a prominent but not yet politically dominant family. His older brother, Joseph P. Kennedy Jr., was widely viewed as the family’s political hope. If JFK had died in 1943, he would have been remembered as a war hero, perhaps posthumously decorated, and his father, Joseph P. Kennedy Sr., might have publicized his sacrifice. However, Joseph Jr. was still alive at that time and remained the intended political heir until his own death in 1944. If both brothers had died (as would have happened historically with Joe Jr.’s 1944 death), the Kennedy political dynasty might never have risen to national prominence.

Without JFK:

There would likely have been no President Kennedy in 1961. The 1960 election would probably have been won by Richard Nixon, since Kennedy’s narrow victory depended on his personal appeal, Catholic outreach, strong debate performance, and machine support in key states. A Nixon presidency beginning in 1961 would have altered Cold War dynamics at a critical moment.

The Bay of Pigs invasion might still have occurred under Nixon, but its handling could have differed. More significantly, the Cuban Missile Crisis might not have unfolded in the same way. Kennedy’s cautious yet firm management—especially his resistance to immediate air strikes and invasion—was central to the peaceful resolution. A different president might have escalated more aggressively or, alternatively, avoided the specific chain of events that led to the crisis. The risk of nuclear confrontation in 1962 could have been either higher or differently timed.

Domestically, civil rights progress might have taken a different trajectory. Kennedy’s administration was initially cautious but increasingly supportive of civil rights legislation by 1963. Lyndon B. Johnson’s presidency—and the Civil Rights Act of 1964—were enabled by Kennedy’s assassination and the political momentum that followed. If Nixon had been president instead, civil rights legislation may have advanced more slowly, or in a different form, depending on congressional dynamics.

The space race might also have unfolded differently. Kennedy’s 1961 commitment to landing a man on the Moon before the decade’s end was pivotal. Another president might not have framed the Apollo program as a national imperative at that scale or speed.

Culturally, the symbolism of “Camelot,” the generational shift to youthful leadership, and the enduring legacy of Kennedy’s assassination in 1963 would never have existed. The political careers of Robert F. Kennedy and Ted Kennedy would likely have been reshaped or diminished without JFK’s presidency as a catalyst.

In short, JFK’s death in 1943 would not have immediately altered World War II, but it likely would have changed the outcome of the 1960 election, reshaped early 1960s Cold War crises, altered the pace of civil rights and space policy, and prevented one of the most defining presidencies—and assassinations—of 20th‑century America.

items.question: What If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981?
human_answers: The core problem with these discussions is that you wind up with a lot of people who had personal experience with home computers imagining their home computer was a long-term viable platform particularly killed by the IBM PC. The inherent market dynamic was, instead, that all the home computers were doomed to extinction at the hands of the standard business personal computer platform. It is businesses that care about backward compatibility with their internal installed base, while the home computer user market has an observable willingness to abandon old platforms and adopt new ones. This means home-targeted versions of the business platform can easily be adopted by the home market, while business-targeted versions of home platforms can only get adopted by businesses if they have a specific compelling business advantage. And then, as soon as the business platform clones the advantage, the home platform is again on the defensive. Home platforms are thus in an inherently weak position, and will be smashed flat by the standard business platform. And, well, there was already a standard business personal computer platform in 1980-1981 -- the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. You could buy that platform as an Osborne 1, or as a Xerox 820, or from any of dozens of other of other makers. You even had the Microsoft Softcard (originally, "Z-80 Softcard", but Zilog complained) which used an Apple II as a host for a 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The major problem that the CP/M-80 platform had going forward was that it had run up against the 64k RAM addressing limit of the 8080/8085/Z80, at a time when RAM prices had dropped enough that it was entirely practical to buy more. And since none of the chipmakers had had the sense to make a 8080-compatible processor with wider addressing, the only real way forward was the 8086/8088, since 8080 assembly code could be easily machine-translated into 8086 code. Everybody was just waiting on Digital Research to get CP/M-86 out. The IBM PC then arrived, with an OS that was arguably even more compatible in its system calls with CP/M-80, and the ability to use all the RAM anybody could practically afford. (Even if Gates never said 640K was enough for anybody, in 1981 that was true. Indeed, the first version of the PC's BIOS had a 544K limit.) It was the perfectly natural successor to the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The IBM endorsement made the transition smoother, and did have some secondary consequences (killing the S-100 bus, for example), but the true key to the IBM PC's success is that it was the natural successor-host for a software ecosystem that had grown up on top of the Altair 8800. What happens in the absence of the IBM PC is simple enough. Digital Research will release CP/M-86. At which point the CP/M-86 systems take over the business market, and eventually all the home computer platforms are killed by the multi-manufacturer business standard, just as in the original timeline.

As I understand it, the IBM machine was intended as an 'intelligent terminal' for their mainframes .. Businesses already had mainframes & dumb terminals but because the terminals were dumb the mainframe had to do everything - which led to limits on the numbers - and whilst IBM would be happy to sell (rent) you another mainframe they then run into the problem of getting the mainframes to talk 'seamlessly' to each other ... so IBM work on evermore powerful / more expensive mainframes as the number of users go up .. If, however, you can off-load some of the 'housekeeping' (things like deciding how to repaint the screen as the user edits a file, without the entire screen contents having to be resent from the mainframe, for example) onto the terminal, you can roll out cheap low end mainframes (at the same cost as the high end ones, naturally) able to cope with 100's more users .. Other companies wanted to 'get in on' IBM's business but had difficulties building mainframes as powerful as the IBM ones = thus, sooner or later, some-one else is going to come up with the concept of 'intelligent terminals' .. after which the PC becomes more or less inevitable ..

items.model_answer:
If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981, personal computing would still have developed—but likely more slowly, more fragmented, and under different corporate leadership.

In 1981, the personal computer market already existed. Companies like Apple, Commodore, Atari, and Tandy were selling machines aimed at hobbyists, educators, and small businesses. However, the IBM PC did something distinctive: it legitimized personal computing for mainstream business. IBM’s reputation reassured corporate buyers who had previously relied on mainframes and minicomputers. Without IBM’s entry, large firms might have delayed adopting desktop computers, relying longer on centralized systems and terminals. The shift toward decentralized office computing could have been slower.

Equally important was the IBM PC’s open architecture. IBM used off‑the‑shelf components and published technical specifications, which allowed other companies to create “IBM-compatible” clones. This fostered intense competition, drove prices down, and standardized hardware around what became the Wintel (Windows + Intel) ecosystem. Without the IBM PC as a de facto standard, the market likely would have remained fragmented among incompatible systems—Apple, Commodore, and others—each with proprietary designs. Software development would have been more costly and divided across platforms, potentially slowing the rise of a unified software industry.

Microsoft’s trajectory would also have been very different. MS-DOS, licensed to IBM and then to clone makers, became the foundation of Microsoft’s dominance. Without the IBM PC standard, Microsoft might have remained primarily a programming language company or played a smaller role in operating systems. Apple, by contrast, might have gained a larger share of the business market, especially if it had adapted more quickly to corporate needs. Alternatively, another firm—perhaps a Japanese electronics company or a different American manufacturer—could have emerged as the standard-setter.

The absence of a dominant IBM-compatible platform might also have altered the development of the internet era. A more diverse hardware ecosystem could have encouraged earlier emphasis on cross-platform software and open standards, but it might also have slowed mass adoption due to incompatibility and higher costs. The rapid spread of affordable clone PCs in the late 1980s and 1990s helped expand computer ownership globally; without that price competition, household computing might have remained more limited for longer.

In short, personal computing would almost certainly still have expanded, driven by technological momentum and consumer demand. But without the IBM PC, the industry would likely have been less standardized, corporate adoption slower, Microsoft less dominant, and the structure of the modern technology sector significantly different.

items.question: What If No P51 Bomber Escort?
human_answers: The P-51B/C/D was clearly a better dogfighter at medium and low altitude, but at 25-30,000ft the R-2800 engine in the P-47 maintained power even better than the Packard Merlin and the DB-605 engine in the Bf-109G. The P-47 was made to rule at 30,000ft. The P-47 shootdown almost the same number of fighters as the P-51, and the highest scoring USAAF groups in the ETO were P-47 units. Yes, the P-51 was shooting down more German fighters from mid-1944 on but that was because the P-51 was given the high-altitude job where they would encounter more enemy fighters while the P-47 was given most of the low altitude work like CAS, and interdiction missions. This is not to take away any credit from the P-51 but in most histories the Mustang gets the glory, and the Thunderbolt is relegated to being a ground support aircraft. The Mustang was clearly given the right name. She was fast and graceful and could dance with the best of them. The Thunderbolt had the right name as well. She was a warhorse that could absorb more punishment and bring her pilot home while raining thunder on the enemy. The P-38 Lightning is another also run for more complicated reasons, but she has her admirers for many reasons. And in 4th place the P-40 Warhawk held the line from 1940-43. Strangely it's the Mustang and the Flying Tigers Warhawk that are remembered best.

Hence my post about Big Week, P-47 provided 80% of the escort fighters during that effort. I doubt very many people realize that. P-38 is an interesting plane, read an interview with a high scoring German ace who said that provided it was being flown by a pilot who knew how to handle it he thought the P-38 was the toughest Allied fighter he faced. It also presented the Japanese with a difficult tactical problem in that it flew higher and faster than both the Zero and the Oscar. General Kenney liked it best because of the two engines. His pilots flew a lot of missions over water and he appreciated what two engines provided in that sense. General Chennault did not like for the same reason. He was at the ass end of a long logistics chain in a lower priority theater. To him two engines just meant twice the engine maintenance. The P-40 deserves much more credit that it gets. Only the P-51 and P-47 were produced in greater numbers (for US fighters), it was used extensively in the MTO, PTO, and CBI theaters well into 1944 and it was used by more Allied air forces than any other fighter. It was not a thoroughbred by it was definitely a work horse and sometimes that is what you need.

Cost to buy and operate the P-47 was not a factor - USA have had the money, material and fuel. They were after all buying and using the P-38, that offered no savings in any category. P-47 was made in more than 15000 copies. The P-47 was turned into a ground attack aircraft after the fact, and fact being that Merlin Mustang was rangier, a bit faster and a better climber. A combination of the P-51 getting the drop tanks earlier, and the better mileage on internal fuel made it the premier LR fighter of the war. Two very common 75 gal drop tanks make the P-51 going much further than if two 75 gal drop tanks are carried by the P-47 or the P-38. Some mix-up happened there. As-is, it could not do the job. With a bit of foresight, it might've come close. People at USAAF will need to request that P-47 is outfitted with wing racks from day one (ie. already in 1942, so it is debugged and ready for 1943), and there should be the drive to increase the internal fuel tankage. In OTL, the 1st increase was achieved by removing the stuff between the main tank and the top of fuselage so the main tank can get bigger, now with 270 instead of 205 US gals. That change upped the internal fuel tankage to 370 gals, that, together with 2x 150 gal drop tanks, enabled the theoretical 600 mile combat radius under the demanding ETO rules (that included cruising at more than 300 mph TAS at 25000 ft). There is also the need for the actual drop tanks to be available in the UK, with clear contracts with the suppliers. The know 'bubbletop' P-47Ds were the 1st with the main tank being at 270 gals. If there was the earlier go with adding some fuel tanks in the wings - even if it is not a 'surgery' as what was done with the P-47N, but perhaps 2x 50 gals? - together with a drop tank under the fuselage, the radius would've been increased even more, equaling the best P-51D values.

The P 47 was an incredible fighter and despite it's sheer size was fairly good in a dogfight. The P-51 Mustang was until the Rolls Royce Merlin was used a low level fighter at best. The V-1710 engine was fine but needed the two stage supercharger and the like which did happen it just took time. Drop Tanks and education on how to achieve maximum range needed to happen in order to make the Mustand what it became. The P-51 B was the start of the Merlin engines and gave it excellent high altitude performance. The P-47 on the other hand did not need an engine swap to be effective. Instead doctrine and production numbers made the difference. The most important use of the daylight bomber offensive, was the decimation of the Luftwaffe and this occurred in measurable ways. The P-38 was suffering from poor pilot training and tactics. THe presence of 3 high performance fighters whose abilities compliment each other is very desirable.
items.original_question: What if No P51 Bomber Escort? From Jan 1944 the Merlin engined P51 could escort the Bombers all the way to Berlin and beyond and destroyed the Luftwaffe in doing so. However, I would argue the P47 could have done the same job but The P47 did not get the escort gig because it was twice the cost and it was a superb ground attack aircraft. twice the cost in construction and fuel consumption. Really the game changer was the drop tank although the P51 was the best host for them by far I think of the P51 as the sleek technical European sports car sipping fuel, with the P47 as a brute, "cubes is everything", American muscle car guzzling gas like there was no tomorrow. The POD would be North American builds P40s instead of creating the new P51 design for the British. The distance the P-47 could cover evolved rapidly as new tanks were engineered: Early 1943 (No tanks): ~175 miles. (Could barely reach the Dutch border). Mid 1943 (75-gal belly tank): ~230 miles. (Reached Antwerp/Ruhr Valley). Late 1943 (108-gal belly tank): ~375 miles. (Reached Frankfurt). Early 1944 (Maximal 3-tank setup): 475–500+ miles. The P47 did not get the escort gig because it was twice the cost and it was a superb ground attack aircraft with its radial engine. OTL the Mustang was a dangerous aircraft to strafe German airfields while a much better dogfighter than the P47 [fixed after tomo mentioned]. I believe more P51s lost to ground fire than air combat. But I would argue that the Mustang was the best solution to the need for an escort, but the P47 could have done the job. Standardising on the P47 would simplify the training and operations of the fighter arm but at double the cost would it have been as effective and escort in numbers? I look forward to your thoughts.

If the P‑51 Mustang had not been available as a long‑range bomber escort, the Allied strategic bombing campaign over Europe would likely have been far less effective and far more costly, with significant consequences for the timing and shape of the war in Europe.

Before the P‑51’s arrival in late 1943, U.S. bombers such as the B‑17 and B‑24 attempted deep raids into Germany without continuous fighter escort. Earlier escorts like the P‑47 Thunderbolt and P‑38 Lightning lacked sufficient range to accompany bombers all the way to key targets such as Berlin. As a result, unescorted bombers suffered devastating losses to German fighters and anti‑aircraft defenses, as seen in missions like the Schweinfurt–Regensburg raids. Losses were so severe that the U.S. Army Air Forces temporarily curtailed deep penetration raids.

The P‑51, especially when fitted with drop tanks and powered by the Rolls‑Royce Merlin engine, could escort bombers all the way to and from deep German targets. Crucially, it did more than just fly alongside bombers: it aggressively sought out and destroyed German fighters, gradually achieving air superiority over the Reich. This attrition of the Luftwaffe’s fighter force, combined with attacks on aircraft factories and fuel supplies, crippled Germany’s ability to defend its airspace by 1944.

Without the P‑51, several major effects are likely. First, bomber losses would have remained unsustainably high, forcing the Allies either to scale back deep strategic bombing or to accept enormous casualties in men and aircraft. The U.S. might have shifted more heavily toward night bombing (as the British did) or focused on peripheral targets within limited escort range. Second, the Luftwaffe would likely have remained stronger for longer. A less degraded German fighter force in 1944 could have posed a much greater threat during the D‑Day landings and the subsequent campaign in Western Europe, potentially increasing Allied casualties and complicating the invasion.

Third, the destruction of Germany’s oil industry and transportation networks—key factors in crippling the Wehrmacht in 1944–45—might have been delayed or less complete. German forces on both the Eastern and Western Fronts depended heavily on fuel and rail mobility. If these systems had been more intact, Germany might have prolonged the war in Europe, possibly into 1946, though it is unlikely to have changed the ultimate outcome given the overwhelming industrial and manpower superiority of the Allies and the Soviet Union.

In short, without the P‑51 bomber escort, the Allied air campaign would have been bloodier, slower, and less decisive. The war in Europe probably would still have ended in Allied victory, but at greater cost and potentially after a longer and more difficult campaign.
