items.question: What If the Holy Roman Empire never existed? How would Europe have turned out?
human_answers: What if the Holy Roman Empire never existed? How would Europe have turned out? The Holy Roman Empire was the legacy of the Roman Empire. The Roman Empire (as opposed to the HOLY Roman Empire) plunged Western Europe into the Middle Ages, from 476 CE (the razing of Rome by the Goths/ the collapse of Rome/ the retrenchment of Rome) to 1266 CE Marco Polo (goes to China) to 1492 CE (the discovery of the Americas by Spain/ starting Mercantilism & Colonialism). It is hard to put a firm date on the latter time when the Middle Ages ended. The role of the Roman Empire. The Roman Empire provided a conduit for a Pax Romana, that, in turn, provided for a common culture and trade from Wales in the West to Asia Minor in the East. From Germania in the North to Numidia in the South. The Roman Empire essentially lined the Mediterranian Sea. When the Roman Empire came apart, we saw the balkanization of Europe, EXCEPT for the Holy Roman Empire. We see the various raiding groups causing the fortification and (for the Roman Catholic Church the Monasticism, of Europe, as the social order broke down and people’s view of their then-world became increasingly insular! The exception of the Holy Roman Empire and the Church of Rome were the phoenix that arose out of ashes of the Roman Empire and that was the Roman Catholic Church, aka The Vatican, and that formed the Holy Roman Empire (the geopolitical extension of the Catholic Church.) Which was basically Italy and Germany. There will those who will bring up the Byzantine Empire. You are right but let’s keep this simple, shall we? I believe the questioner was asking about Western Europe and it is that, to which I am addressing my comments. You are free to write your own answer for the Moorish perspective. The Vatican itself had a bigger, but weaker, hold over Western Europe. in contrast to the Holy Roman Empire. In large part, that is that a King needed the Pope’s support & backing to rule. Excommunication was a death sentence to a King’s reign. Power flowed from the Vatican to the King and down thru the nobles. Less is Moor! It is at this point, that I must bring in the Moors, so I might mention that the Middle East was blockaded, as a route to the Orient. Columbus was hired to find a western route to the Orient, by the Spanish royal couple, Ferdinand & Isabella, to end-run that blockade of the Middle East, the Moors having just expelled from Spain! Columbus’s success drew the rulers and merchant of many West Europeans outlook of the world into a more colonial view of the world. Mercantilism & Colonialism. Mercantilism is the economic view of getting resources from colonies and selling finished goods to those colonies. Colonies are a political view of establishing colonies. This race for territory caused a lot, A LOT, of tensions between the nations of Western Europe, not to mention the colony and mother country. The land grab leads to navies, armies, and the settlements to protect trade routes and exploit the resources of those colonies in the Americas, Africa, and Asia. This leads, in turn, to mutual defense treaties (the bifurcation of us vs them. In 1517 CE, Martin Luther & his 95 Thesis’s which begins the beginning of the Reformation. The Vatican begins to lose its grip over Western Europe. Competing Churches no longer recognize the Pope as the supreme authority and Governments rapidly follow suit, leading to even more tension. In 1806 CE, Napolean puts an end to the Holy Roman Empire. Italy and Germany split into principalities, that eventually evolved into modern nations of Italy and Germany. Nationalism took root! The modern era summarized. This tensions reached a flashpoint when a Serbian nationalist assassinated the Archduke of Austria and his wife! All those mutual defense treaties came in to play and WW I began. This led to the Czar and his family being overthrown in Russia, leading in turn to communism and the Soviet Union. The land grab and mutual defense treaties, after WW II, which encouraged colonies to break away and assert their independence. The Cold War. The dissolution of the USSR. Modern times. When it is all said and done. How would it be without the Holy Roman Empire? In a word “Different!” The social and historical order would be changed. Like dominos falling into each other into each other, the dominions of Europe would be reprioritized. We got the history we got because things happened as they did. You start to tug on the woof and weave of time, time will unravel like a cheap sweater, and then all bets are off, about how that history evolves. You can hate the Roman Empire, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Vatican, but they got us where we are and none can say if an alternative would be better or worse!

Question: What if the Holy Roman Empire never existed? How would Europe have turned out? Details: Would Europe perhaps have had 1 or 2 Super States comparable to China in the Middle East? I’m not sure I ‘get’ the question. Charlemagne’s empire, often regarded as the origin of the Holy Roman Empire, was the nearest Western Europe came to a super state. If the Pope had not decided to crown Charlemagne Emperor in 800, so he continued as King of the Franks, as he had been since 774, I can’t really see that would have made much difference. The break-up, shortly after Charlemagne’s death, had nothing to do with his title of Emperor. Partible inheritance had a lot to do with, but even with primogeniture, the Empire might not have been very stable. We know, from the Oaths of Strasbourg (842) that France and Germany already had well established separate languages by then, even though the ruling classes were all of German origin. They also had very distinct cultural histories, with France’s institutions inherited from the old Roman Empire, which Germany had always stood outside. The Holy Roman Empire was refounded as a powerful state by Otto the Great in 962. This incarnation never included France, but did include Germany (plus some surrounding lands) and what contemporaries called Italy (the northern half of what we call Italy). This empire held together as a powerful and, by the standards of the day, quite co-ordinated entity, until the fall of the Hohenstaufen in 1254. I can see how, had the Hohenstaufen not fallen, there was a potential for it to develop into a superstate bestriding much of Western Europe, perhaps by conquest, but more likely by inheritance. Something like Charles V’s empire, but sooner, and based on a much more powerful and united Germany. Its contemporaries could see that potential too, especially when it inherited and took over Sicily (including the southern half of today’s Italy). That is one reason why some of them combined to bring it down when the opportunity presented itself. How the Empire not existing could help that process, though, I’m really not sure. Eastern Europe, of course, had and has its superstate, Russia.

Counterfactual premise A world without the Holy Roman Empire (HRE) means removing a political entity that, from roughly 800–1806, linked a patchwork of central European duchies, bishoprics, free cities and principalities under an elective imperial crown claiming Roman continuity. “Never existed” can be interpreted in two ways: (A) Charlemagne never unified Francian/German lands into an empire in 800, so no imperial tradition develops; or (B) a united central-imperial polity is attempted but fails early and never reconstitutes. Both lead to similar broad consequences: a much weaker supra‑regional institution in Central Europe, earlier fragmentation or alternative unifiers, different church–state relations, altered balance among France, Poland, Italy, the Baltic and the Ottoman frontier, and big effects on state formation, law, religion and culture. Core structural consequences (high level) Greater political fragmentation in the German-speaking lands for longer, accelerating emergence of numerous small sovereign states or city-states with stronger local sovereignty. Without an imperial crown as a focal institution, imperial law, imperial diets and the symbolic framework that mediated overlordship are gone. Earlier consolidation by other regional powers. France would face a more fragmented eastern neighbor; Brandenburg/Prussia, Poland, Bavaria, and Austria would compete to fill the power vacuum. That competition would likely produce a different map: some larger territorial states (Prussia or Poland–Lithuania) could expand sooner and further; alternatively, many microstates persist under shifting suzerainties. Different Church–state dynamics. The HRE’s peculiar relationship with the papacy (lay investiture conflict, imperial coronations, imperial protection of papal interests at times) disappears, changing ecclesiastical politics in Italy and Central Europe. Local princes may gain ecclesiastical autonomy faster; church reform movements and the timing/location of conflicts with Rome shift. Italy’s fragmentation intensifies long-term. The HRE historically provided a counterweight to papal and northern Italian city ambitions. Without imperial intervention, northern Italian communes and the papacy consolidate power in different patterns; the peninsula could see an earlier and more decisive rise of maritime republics or stronger papal states. The map of colonization, warfare and alliances in the later early modern period shifts, because a major central European diplomatic player is missing. European coalitions against France, the Ottomans, or in colonial rivalry form differently. Political and military consequences Rise of alternative hegemonies: Brandenburg/Prussia or Austria might either not arise as single hegemonic states or would develop different identities. If no imperial legitimacy constrains them, dynasties could centralize quicker or be absorbed by neighbors. A strong Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth could expand west into Silesia and Bohemia absent imperial claims, creating a large Poland-centered bloc. The balance against the Ottomans alters: the HRE’s patchwork provided troops, fortresses and political organization to resist Ottoman expansion in Hungary and the Balkans. Without a coordinating imperial structure, response to Ottoman advance could be slower and more regionally uneven; the Ottomans might consolidate greater gains in Central Europe earlier, or conversely local powers could carve defensive coalitions independent of an emperor. Warfare and military innovation diffuse differently. Habsburg dynastic networks that used imperial offices to bind Central Europe would be less effective; their dynastic power would need other bases (landed holdings, marriage alliances), shifting the locus of Habsburg power possibly more toward Spain/Italy earlier or less central in German lands. Religion and the Reformation Protestant Reformation dynamics change substantially. In the historical HRE, the refusal or acceptance of imperial enforcement, the Peace of Augsburg (1555) and the Thirty Years’ War (1618–48) were mediated by imperial institutions. Without an empire: Local rulers might adopt confessional changes with fewer supra‑regional constraints, producing a more mosaic religious map more quickly. Continental confessional wars might be less sweeping but more localized; or they might be replaced by prolonged border conflicts between rising states (e.g., Sweden, Poland, France) rather than an empire-centered Thirty Years’ War. The Peace of Westphalia’s state-sovereignty principles would arise differently or later; the concept of sovereign territorial states might develop earlier as local rulers assert final authority over religion and law. Legal, economic and cultural effects Legal fragmentation and local autonomy accelerate. The imperial legal framework (Imperial Chamber Court, Reichstag) that moderated disputes and preserved rights for imperial estates is absent, so legal pluralism strengthens and regional customary law matters more. Urban and mercantile development. Free imperial cities were historically important nodes. Without imperial status, some cities either fall under territorial princes faster (reducing urban autonomy) or secure different international protections (alliances with Venice, Hanseatic League, or France). The Hanseatic League and Italian maritime republics may gain or lose relative influence depending on territorial pressure from expanded states. Cultural and intellectual flows persist but different patronage networks emerge. Universities, monastic orders and the printing press continue to diffuse ideas; without imperial patronage, cultural centers may cluster more strongly in distinct courts (Prussia, France, Poland, Italian states) and in free cities that find other patrons. Colonial and global consequences Central European absence as a unified actor likely does not dramatically alter early Iberian and later British/Dutch colonization because those were maritime powers. However: A weaker or more fragmented Habsburg base could reduce Spanish/Habsburg coordination across Europe, affecting Habsburg capacities in the 16th–17th centuries. Migration patterns to the Americas and colonies may change: German-speaking emigration might be more regionally driven by small principalities rather than imperial policy, altering settlement patterns in North America and the Caribbean. Military manpower supply for colonial wars differs; mercenary markets in Central Europe could expand, influencing wars abroad. Long-term nation-building and modern map (plausible scenarios) Scenario A — Early microstate Europe Persistent extreme fragmentation: dozens of sovereign German-speaking principalities and city-states survive into the 19th century. France and a stronger Prussia (or a stronger Austria that never consolidated imperial claims) dominate; German unification is delayed or takes a different form (confederation under French or Austrian influence, or a northern confederation led by Prussia emerges later as in real history but with different borders). Industrialization in German lands is uneven; some city-states industrialize quickly, others lag. Scenario B — Alternative unifier rises Prussia (Brandenburg) or a Polish–Silesian union becomes the dominant central European state earlier. If Prussia unifies German lands sooner without an imperial counterweight, a unified German nation-state might appear before 1871, changing the Napoleonic era and the 19th-century balance. If Poland expands west, a large Central European Commonwealth alters Russo‑Prussian dynamics. Scenario C — Stronger regional empires elsewhere Without imperial symbolic legitimacy in Central Europe, dynasties like the Habsburgs pivot toward Italy/Spain and build more coherent maritime/peninsular empires, or they lose ground to France and the Ottomans. The Ottoman Empire may hold more territory in Hungary and the Balkans for longer. Effects on modern Europe (concise) Germany’s path to nationhood changes: the German Empire of 1871 might not exist as known; German-speaking unity could be delayed, achieved under different leadership, or remain fragmented into smaller states in the 20th century. Borders of modern states shift: Poland, Czech lands (Bohemia), Silesia, Bavaria and the Austrian core could belong to different polities or be partitioned differently in the 18th–19th centuries. The ideological legacy of the HRE (mixed sovereignty, legal pluralism, imperial law) that influenced Western legal thought is weaker; the Westphalian state system might crystallize differently, potentially strengthening territorial sovereignty earlier. European wars of the 17th–19th centuries reconfigure: alliances without an imperial center produce different coalition patterns against France, Britain, and the Ottomans, producing alternative outcomes in the Napoleonic and world wars. Key takeaway Removing the Holy Roman Empire shifts Europe from a semi‑centralized, symbolic imperial order to a more fragmented or differently united Central Europe. The most probable outcomes are stronger competition among regional powers (Prussia, Austria, Poland, France, the Ottomans), earlier and deeper political fragmentation in German lands, altered religious and legal settlements, and a different timeline for European state consolidation and balance of power. Exact borders and events are highly sensitive to contingent decisions—small dynastic marriages, battles, or success of a single ambitious ruler could produce radically different maps—so the counterfactual space is wide, but the themes above are robust across plausible variants.

There is no such thing as a total polity vacuum. As an example: defeated Germany in 1945 was occupied, divided and ruled by the victors in specific zones. Lower level German administration (in villages, cities) and courts of justice, never ceased to exist. Similarly, without the Holy Roman Empire, another polity would have taken the place. A confederation of German states, perhaps, with or without a loose central authority. Nothing really different from the HRE, except for one point: there would be much less friction with the East Roman Empire (Constantinople), which always claimed exclusivity in the use of “Roman” and supremacy in title and political protocol. Could such a better understanding between Byzantium and Central Europe have avoided the Schism of the Church in 1054 ? Probably. A united Christianity, under increased influence of the Byzantine ecclesiastic model, might have avoided the struggle between Papacy and European kings, might also have avoided the Protestant Reformation. Last but not least, crusades in much better coordination with Constantinople, better and lasting results. And no Turks in Europe , not even in Asia Minor…

If the Holy Roman Empire had never existed, Europe would likely have developed with fewer layers of political fragmentation in Central Europe, earlier consolidation of territorial states, and potentially different balances of power between France, Italy, and the German lands. However, many of the underlying forces—feudalism, dynastic politics, Church authority, and geographic constraints—would still have shaped the continent in comparable ways.

The Holy Roman Empire (HRE), founded in 962, was less a centralized empire than a loose confederation of duchies, bishoprics, free cities, and kingdoms under an elected emperor. Its existence institutionalized political fragmentation in Central Europe, especially in the German-speaking regions and northern Italy. Without it, the territory that became Germany might have consolidated earlier into a more unified kingdom, similar to France or England. Alternatively, it might have fractured permanently into several medium-sized kingdoms rather than hundreds of semi-sovereign states under imperial structure.

One major difference would likely concern Italy. The HRE’s claims over northern and central Italy tied the region to German politics for centuries, contributing to prolonged instability and conflict between imperial and papal factions. Without imperial involvement, northern Italy might have formed more durable regional kingdoms or leagues earlier, possibly allowing for stronger political unity centuries before the 19th century. Papal temporal power might also have evolved differently without the constant tension between emperor and pope.

The HRE also acted as a structural counterweight to France. Because Central Europe was divided, France could expand eastward at various points, but it also faced an imperial bloc in diplomacy. If no empire had existed and Germany had unified early, Europe might have seen a powerful German kingdom emerge by the High Middle Ages—potentially rivaling or even dominating France much earlier. Conversely, if fragmentation had continued without imperial cohesion, France might have expanded more aggressively into the Rhineland and beyond.

Religiously, the Protestant Reformation unfolded in a political environment shaped by the Empire’s semi-autonomous princes. The imperial structure allowed Lutheranism and other Protestant movements to survive because local rulers could adopt them under the principle later formalized as “cuius regio, eius religio.” Without the Empire’s decentralized framework, either Protestantism might have been suppressed more effectively by a strong centralized monarchy, or religious wars might have taken a different, possibly more binary form, like those in France or England.

The Thirty Years’ War, which devastated Central Europe, was deeply tied to imperial constitutional struggles. Without the HRE, such a pan-German conflict might not have occurred in the same way, potentially sparing the region massive demographic and economic losses. This could have allowed Central Europe to industrialize or consolidate politically earlier.

In the long run, the delayed unification of Germany in 1871 was partly a legacy of imperial fragmentation. Without the HRE’s long institutional afterlife, a German nation-state might have emerged centuries earlier—or, alternatively, the region might have remained permanently divided like Italy before the 19th century. In either case, the timing and character of modern European power politics would have changed significantly, possibly altering the causes or alignments of World War I.

Overall, the absence of the Holy Roman Empire would most likely have meant a less formally fragmented Central Europe and a different balance of power between France, Italy, and the German lands. Yet Europe would still have been shaped by geography, feudal structures, dynastic marriages, and Church authority. The map would have looked different, but the underlying competitive state system that defined European history would probably still have emerged—just along somewhat altered lines and timelines.

items.question: What If the Roman Empire never fell and lived to the year 2020?
human_answers: Note: Parts of this answer will be copied from this one . However, this is a different scenario than that one. Note: I do not claim that this answer is realistic, nor that everything would happen the way I say it would. This is, of course, impossible to predict. Anyway, the point of divergence here is 378 AD, with the battle of Adrianople. Battle of Adrianople You see, Rome could have won this battle quite decisively. They had numerical parity, if not superiority, to the Gothic forces. They had great heavy cavalry. Valens had a large amount of additional reinforcements marching in from the west as well. They likely would have arrived within the next few days. Had the two forces linked up, they would have likely beaten the Goths. Why did I have the Romans win at Adrianople? The Roman defeat at Adrianople and the resulting Gothic invasions devastated the Balkans, to the point where they were somewhat depopulated. This is avoided in this timeline. This also avoids the Goths rising up in revolt within the Empire later on. With the Balkans in a much better position, the Romans are able to largely keep the Huns at bay, forcing them west. The Huns were defeated in battle by the Western Romans and their allies in 451 AD, so I could see the Eastern Romans doing the same here. Next, Theodosius the Great recognizes Eunegius as Emperor in 394, rather than killing and deposing him. This avoids the problem of Honorius becoming Emperor and also doesn’t kill over a third of the western army. Eunegius agrees to let Flavius Stilicho become Magister Militum of the west in exchange for being recognized as Emperor. Stilicho would survive longer in this timeline due to Honorius not rising to power, allowing him to better contain the barbarians invading the Empire. He would represent a bridge between the barbarians living within the Empire, allowing them to be more easily assimalated and showing that the two could coexist. Flavius Aetius would also survive longer, giving Rome a strong military leader to hold the Empire together. Next, Majorian is not betrayed in 460 AD, and his fleet is not destroyed. This allows him to retake North Africa, giving Western Rome fresh sources of manpower, taxes, food, and resources. Majorian finds out about Ricimier’s plots and has him executed. His replacement would be loyal and competent. Majorian would stabalize Italy and North Africa, and implement his reforms to the imperial administration. This would make the Empire more stable. Majorian would implement laws to whip the decedant and lazy upper class back into shape, reinvigorate pride in the Roman state, and reintroduce native Italians into the army. Majorian’s successor, likely Julius Nepos, would continue his reforms, enforcing and expanding upon them. Roman Empire in 460 AD. In this timeline, Carthage is under Roman rule as well. Under Majorian’s successors, Gaul and most of Hispania would still be lost, but the Empire would survive. Julius Nepos comes to power in the mid-late 470s, continuing the reforms of Majorian and strengthening the Empire. He would fortify the borders and choose a competent successor, who would continue the reforms of Majorian and Nepos. Majorian, Nepos, and their successors would recognize that the Empire could not rely on slavery, and that it needed to bolster its population in order to survive. Therefore, they would implement more efficient farming practices and the use of technology such as water wheels and mills in order to make the production of flour more efficient. They would also update architectural codes and improve living standards in order to increase stability and keep more people alive and healthy. They would massively revamp sanitation systems to reduce the risk of disease and improve healthcare for pregnant mothers in order to bolster the population further. They would also choose a competent successor, who would likely free most remaining slaves to increase the conscriptable, taxable population. Barbagel water mill complex During this time monuments and architecture would be restored. Propaganda would hearken back to the old days and the resilience of the Roman people, reinvigorating pride in the Empire. Leo I in the East would die a few years later than in our timeline, helping out the West. The West largely goes on as a regional power until Justinian comes along. He would officially reunify the East and West, although there would still be two emperors. Without Italy being devastated by the Gothic wars, its population thrives, and the Roman spirit is reignited in the East as well. Justinian implements the reforms of the West all across the Empire, and Rome reaches a new technological golden age. Hispania and southern Gaul are retaken for the Empire, and the whole of North Africa up to the Atlantic is under Roman control as well. The Justinian Plague is still devastating, but with the improved sanitation and without the devastation of the Gothic wars, Rome is still going strong. The Plague would drive demand for labor up as the population declines, allowing the middle class to grow and seeing the further implementation of technology into the everyday lives of Romans. Women would be allowed to hold more jobs and to work in factories, and would slowly gain more power and rights in society from there. In this timeline, with the Balkans secured and giving Rome much greater manpower than it had in our world, Germanus would be able to destroy the Persians at Antioch, making Persia rethink Rome’s weakness. The Persians would sue for peace, restoring the “Eternal Peace” they had signed with Rome not long before. They would have to make several concessions, allowing Rome to fortify the border. In this timeline, Germanus would not have to fight the Ostrogoths in Italy, and would thus not fall ill. He would become Emperor after Justinian, and after him would be Justin Germanus, who would be another competent ruler. These two would further expand on the reforms of their predecessors, upholding them and giving them time to stick. IRL Rome under Justinian With large sources of manpower from North Africa, the Balkans, and Italy, Rome is not percieved as weak by Persia. In this timeline, Phokas would not rise to power and severely weaken the Empire, as Justin Germanus would not order him to camp north of the Danube for the winter. Maurice would still rise to power after Justin, and would be a fairly competent Emperor as he was in our timeline. After Maurice, Heraclius would not want to see the Empire split between Maurice’s sons and would rise to power. Heraclius was also fairly competent. Without Phokas, and with Persia having been stopped by Germanus decades earlier, the Persians wouldn’t attack the Romans. When the Arabs explode out of the Arabian peninsula, Rome would abandon Gaul and lose Hispania and parts of North Africa. However, they would still hold Carthage, Egypt, and the Levant. They’d also lose bits of the northern Balkans to the Slavs and Avars. However, they’d still hold much of the Balkans. Persia, due to not being exhausted by fighting Rome, would be in a stronger position, and would survive the Arab invasions, though with a loss of territory. In the same way Rome was Europe’s shield during the middle ages, Persia would be Rome’s shield, taking blow after blow and lessening the effects of these invasions on the Roman Empire. The balance of power within the Empire would still shift east, with Constantinople being the capital. The Empire would closely resemble the Eastern Roman/Byzantine Empire of our timeline, but with more Latin influence. During this time, northern Europe still largely develops as it did in our timeline, with the Kingdom of the Franks still emerging and splitting. Hispania is still slowly reconquered by the Europeans, but this time the Romans would participate. Eventually they’d end up with what would be Aragon in our timeline. Much of the middle ages in Europe would be Roman tributary states paying the Romans in exchange for protection. The Pope, chafing under Roman rule, would flee and set up a new branch of Christianity, namely Catholicism. The Romans are able to hold back the Turks as well, keeping them out of the Empire. They win at Manzikert. Rome has entered a period of slow but steady decline, as it did in our timeline. It’s still surviving and prospering, but beginning to rot from the inside. The Great Schism never happens, and neither do the Crusades. Rome is one of the most technologically advanced nations on the planet, being near a state of industrialization. They would have rudimentary air conditioning, sanitation, advanded plumbing and running water, all in every apartment building. They would have hospitals and universities. Their military would be formidable. Factory-like complexes would be common, using water power to produce flour and goods. Slavery would come to be regarded as the mark of a less advanced civilization. Basil II would reinvigorate the Empire, bringing back Roman pride and defeating the Bulgars. He would reform the Empire, and leave it in a much stronger position than it was before his reign. In this timeline, he would choose a competent successor, similarly to Germanus and Justinian. Europe and the Middle East in 1025 AD In 1190, the Romans beat the Bulgarians at the battle of Trinova. This leads to Isaac II not being deposed and the Roman army not being demoralized like in our timeline. Alexios III does not rise to power, and the 4th Crusade never happens, as Alexios IV never needs to contact the crusaders to depose Alexios III. The Romans would have good relations with Hungary to the north. In the 1200s, the Mongol invasions would happen. Whatever Persion/Turkish state that would exists east of Rome would take the brunt of the blow, but Rome would still be hit fairly hard. They wouldn’t be devastated, but they wouldn’t be able to brush it off either. The Black Death would also be devastating, but experience with plagues and sanitation would somewhat mitigate the effects. Like the Justinian Plague before, the Black Death would again grow the middle class, increasing their power within society. The Romans would recover. Mongol expansion The world in 1250 The Turks would still carve out an Empire like they did in our timeline, leading to several wars with the Romans. They would very nearly succeed in taking Constantinople in 1453, but Rome would be able to drive them back. Roman propaganda would once again hearken back to the determination of the Roman people and the strength and culture of classical Rome. There would be a resurgance in classical ideas, innovation, and technology and philosophy, as well as the arts. This would spread throughout Europe, sparking the Renaissance. Rome would reconquer what territory it lost to the Turks, and even expand in some places. Constantine XI and his successor would implement broad reforms to protect from invasions and to make it so that the internal rot that had weakened Rome would not happen again. The 100 Years War ends the way it did in our timeline, and Poland-Lithuania still emerges, as does something like the Tutonic Order. In this timeline, they would fight in the Reconquista before eventually getting evicted and moving up to the Baltic region to stamp out paganism there. Europe in 1450 Rome for centuries would dominate East-West trade, leading the Iberian kingdoms impoverished. They would search for new trade routes, and would travel around Africa and eventually find the Americas. Now the race is on to colonize the New World. In the early 16th century, Rome would conquer down to the Horn of Africa and set up client kingdoms. This would give them access to the lucrative Indian Ocean trade routes. Rome at this point would be incredibly advanced, rich, and prosperous. Huge factory complexes and industrial scale agricultural and mining operations would exist. Roman towns and cities would be among the cleanest in the world. By now almost every building would have a flush toilet and sink. Plumbing would be common in towns as well as cities. Gunpowder weapons would be appearing. Analog computers would be used. The printing press would allow ideas to spread rapidly, spreading technology. The world in 1550 Protestantism would be spreading throughout the northern lands of Europe, and in the early 1610s Germany would be ripped apart by religous war. The Hapsburgs would control Austria, Germany, and Spain, and in a bid to exploit the Hapsburg’s weakness, the French, Romans, and Russians would fight them. The Romans and Russians in particular would support the Protestants against the Catholics, who were enemies of Roman Orthodoxy. The war would end with Germany and Spain crippled, the former of which would be reduced to a messy confederation of states. The Romans would annex Hungary. Brandenburg, Bavaria, and Prussia would come to dominate Germany. Meanwhile, for the past few centuries England, Spain, Portugal, Rome, France, and Holland have been setting up colonies in the Americas. The Romans would not partake in the Atlantic Slave Trade, viewing slavery as the mark of a less advanced civilization. The Portugese would colonize Brazil. The French and British colonies would grow fast in the Americas. Meanwhile, Brandenburg would become a dominant power in Germany alongside Bavaria and Prussia. The three would become close allies, hoping to unite Germany. They would attempt to annex Transnistria, leading to the Seven Years War. The world at the start of the Seven Years War The British side of the war would be: Prussia Brandenburg Bavaria Britain Portugal Rome Russia The French side of the war would be: Austria France Spain Persia Poland Holland The war would be even larger here than in our timeline. Russia would move into Poland-Lithuania, gaining territory until the Polish stop them with a defensive trench line. The Romans would move against the Persians/Turks, pushing them back and taking Armenia. They would advance into Arabia. The British and French would fight in the Americas, and the Romans would advance against the Spanish in both the New World and Old World. The British would seize Spanish islands in the Carribean. The armies of Prussia, Bavaria, and Brandenburg initially push the Austrians back, but get bogged down. After the first winter in Europe, spring offensives begin. However, inspired by Poland, the other powers have built trench lines and fortresses, bogging down any advance. The British and French would fight in India. The Dutch would fight the British, hoping to protect their interests in India. After years of brutal war, Poland is carved up by Prussia and Russia. The Americas largely shake out the way they did in our timeline. Austria is weakened. Rome annexes Persia and Arabia entirely. The Romans would industrialize fairly easily, soon after the British. They had the technology, and the Romans were historically nothing if not adaptable, and during the Medieval era were able to change their institutions to fit the changing world around them. The American colonies still become independent following the Great War. Following a trade dispute in the Indian Ocean due to British control of India, relations between Rome and Britain sour. Rome starts to ally with France and supports the Americans in response. They would also support the native tribes, hoping to stop America from threatening Roman interests in the Americas. The Romans would sell Corsica to France just in time for Napoleon to be born, and the Napoleonic wars still happen. Rome allies with France due to soured relations with Britain. When France invades Russia, however, the Romans turn on Napoleon and deal his empire the death blow. However, the other European powers are mad at the Romans, and force territorial concessions. The Romans lose land both at home and overseas, notably in Iberia and Africa. During their time as a Napoleonic ally, the Roman senate would gain much more power, and the Emperor’s power would be reduced. The Emperor would still be powerful, but they would have to share power with the Senate. The world after the Napoleonic Wars The Romans are embittered by this loss of land. Brandenburg and Prussia would rise in power immensely following this war, becoming the dominant forces in Germany. They would become the de-facto leader of the German Confederation, and would eventually unify Germany in the 1860s and 70s during and after the Franco-German war. During the 1850s, a dispute between ethnic Romans and Slavs in the Crimean Peninsula leads to the Crimean War. Russia and Rome would had been traditional allies for centuries by this point, but Russian expansionism would sour relations between the two. The British and French would intervene on Rome’s side, and the war would ultimately not accomplish anything. In the 1870s, France is devastated by the Franco-Prussian war. The Romans take the opportunity to invade and occupy France, a hugely controversial move. They also annex Spain and Portugal, and move deeper into North Africa. Without the French, the British take the Congo and French West Africa and Indochina. France, Spain, and Portugal are all very rebellious, and fight for independence for decades. However, the Romans are determined to hold on to them. The world in 1914 Then comes the 20th century, the graveyard of empires. While many would say that nationalism would rip the Empire apart, I disagree. In our timeline, even after the Roman Empire died in 1453, the people living in the lands it occupied considered themselves Roman up until well into the 19th century. With a much stronger Roman state and culture, Rome would not succumb to nationalism like so many other Empires would. In 1914, a rogue nationalist assasinates Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Everyone in Europe has been itching to beat each other up, and this is a conventient excuse. Austria blames the Romans and declares war. Russia joins Austria. Britain joins the Romans, and Germany joins Russia and Austria. The war is long and unthinkably bloody. Eventually, the United States would get involved. Russia would collapse into revolution and leave the war. Germany and Austria surrender. Austria is carved up. Britain gets Germany’s colonies. Germany is forced to pay heavy reparations. Russia becomes communist. Austria-Hungary is carved up, with the Romans gaining new lands. The world after World War I I fail to see why the Great Depression would not happen in this timeline, and Germany, already suffering after the war, is utterly devastated, like in our timeline. Hitler or someone like him still takes power and institutes the same policies, stirring German nationalists with anti-Semitic and anti-Slavic propaganda. Japan and Germany still ally. In 1939, Hitler invades Poland, sparking another war. He blitzkriegs his way through the low countries and the Balkans, and then attacks the USSR. Japan also goes on the move, attacking Pearl Harbor, the Phillipines, China, Indochina, and the Dutch East Indies. The world mid war Eventually, the Romans begin a counteroffensive and push the Germans out of the Balkans and low countries. The Soviets also launch a counteroffensive, and Germany is defeated. The world immediately after the war The European powers would start decolonizing as the Cold War sets in. The world during the Cold War China still falls to the communists. The wars in Korea and Vietnam still happen. Both sides intervene in countless nations around the world. The USSR would finally collapse in the early ‘90s, but China still develops like it did in our world. The Romans would eventually give up their lands south of the Mediterranean coast in Africa. Rome today would be a constitutional monarchy, with the Emperor being mostly a figurehead. Their opinions would still hold great sway among the Roman people, but actual power would be concentrated in the Senate. It is no longer the single most powerful nation on the planet, but it is still a superpower to be reckoned with. The Roman Empire would occupy the lands of these modern countries: Italy France Belgium Spain Portugal Greece Turkey Romania Moldova Hungary Bosnia Serbia Kosovo Switzerland Georgia Armenia Egypt Syria Lebanon Iraq Iran Saudi Arabia United Arab Emirates Yemen Oman Jordan Israel/Palestine Slovenia Albania Tunisia Montenegro Macedonia Croatia Northern Morocco The coast of Libya The coast of Algeria Madagascar Azerbaijan Some stats: Land area: 11,558,932 square kilometers (2nd largest in the world) GDP: $14,358,470,000,000 (3rd largest in the world) Population: 848,524,000 (3rd largest in the world) Military size: 6,000,000 active personel The world in 2022 The upvotes load before the views

If the Roman Empire had never fallen and survived to 2020, the modern world would look profoundly different, though not necessarily more “ancient.” To survive that long, Rome would have had to adapt—politically, economically, technologically, and culturally—so the result would likely be a continuous but transformed imperial system rather than a frozen classical world.

Politically, Rome would probably have evolved into a constitutional imperial state, much as monarchies in Britain or Japan evolved rather than disappeared. The emperor might remain a symbolic or semi-executive figure, while a representative senate or parliament gradually took on legislative authority. The concept of citizenship, already expansive by late antiquity, could have developed into a unifying imperial identity spanning Europe, North Africa, and parts of the Middle East. Nationalism as we know it might have been weaker or delayed, since many modern European nations emerged from Rome’s collapse.

Religiously and culturally, Christianity—already the empire’s dominant faith by the 4th century—would likely still have shaped its identity, but perhaps without the sharp Catholic–Orthodox divide if political unity had been preserved. The Protestant Reformation might have taken a different form or been avoided if imperial institutions had successfully reformed church corruption from within. Latin, continuously used as an administrative language, could have evolved into a standardized imperial lingua franca, potentially preventing the fragmentation into distinct Romance languages or at least keeping them mutually closer.

Economically and technologically, a stable Mediterranean superstate might have accelerated development by maintaining integrated trade networks across Europe, North Africa, and the Near East. The so‑called “Dark Ages” in Western Europe may not have occurred, allowing earlier advances in science, urbanization, and infrastructure. However, innovation depends on many factors, including competition; a long-standing hegemon might also have slowed change if it suppressed rivals. Whether Rome would have industrialized earlier or later is uncertain, but by 2020 it would almost certainly be technologically modern if it had remained globally competitive.

Colonialism and global power structures would also differ. A unified Roman Empire might have led overseas expansion in a more centralized way, possibly dominating the Americas and parts of Africa as a single imperial project rather than through competing European nation-states. Alternatively, strong eastern trade ties might have focused Rome more toward Asia. The balance of power with China, India, and Islamic civilizations would have shaped global geopolitics in ways hard to predict, but the modern international system of sovereign nation-states might be replaced by a few massive, long-lived imperial federations.

Most significantly, the idea of political legitimacy would differ. Instead of nationalism and popular sovereignty becoming dominant in the 18th and 19th centuries, imperial citizenship and continuity with antiquity might frame modern identity. Law codes around the world would likely be even more deeply rooted in Roman legal tradition than they already are.

In short, a Roman Empire that lasted to 2020 would not resemble marble temples and togas; it would likely be a vast, evolving imperial federation blending ancient institutional continuity with modern technology. The world would probably be more politically consolidated, culturally Mediterranean-centered, and shaped by a continuous Roman legal and administrative tradition rather than by the fragmented nation-state order that emerged after Rome’s fall.

Politically, Rome would probably have evolved into a constitutional imperial state, much as monarchies in Britain or Japan evolved rather than disappeared.
The emperor might remain a symbolic or semi-executive figure, while a representative senate or parliament gradually took on legislative authority.
The concept of citizenship, already expansive by late antiquity, could have developed into a unifying imperial identity spanning Europe, North Africa, and parts of the Middle East.
Nationalism as we know it might have been weaker or delayed, since many modern European nations emerged from Rome’s collapse.

Religiously and culturally, Christianity—already the empire’s dominant faith by the 4th century—would likely still have shaped its identity, but perhaps without the sharp Catholic–Orthodox divide if political unity had been preserved.
The Protestant Reformation might have taken a different form or been avoided if imperial institutions had successfully reformed church corruption from within.

Latin, continuously used as an administrative language, could have evolved into a standardized imperial lingua franca, potentially preventing the fragmentation into distinct Romance languages or at least keeping them mutually closer.

items.question: What If the Roman Empire never fell? How would this change most of our history today?
human_answers: The problem with the previous answer is that it is ahistorical. The Roman Empire did not fall until 1453, when the Ottoman Turks conquered Constantinople. Emperor Constantine had moved the capitol to the Greek city of Byzantium because of its excellent geographic, strategic, and central location, calling it New Rome, although at that point the empire was then split between eastern and western halves until the west collapsed in the fifth century. Subsequently renamed Constantinople, it then became the center of the world and continued long after the city of Rome itself declined sharply as the locus of empire shifted. Attempts, sometimes successful, were made to reclaim parts of the west. Indeed the name of the city itself continued until the cataclysm of World War I. In addition, Justinian was the last Emperor to use Latin rather than Greek, which prevailed for another eight centuries, or far longer than Rome itself. There was never a “Byzantine Empire.” That was a far later German concoction in order to legitimate their own “Holy Roman Empire, which, as Voltaire once said, was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire, What actually existed, as I have suggested elsewhere, was not something “Byzantine,” but rather a Greco-Roman Empire that lasted for a millennium. This is still confused and not well known due to the ignorance and prejudice of northwestern Europeans towards the south. Thus, the Roman Empire did not fall or disappear the way you have been led to believe. In fact, if the empire began with Augustus, the Rome-based portion only lasted for a bit more than four centuries, while the Eastern Roman Empire continued for another thousand years, and all the people in the empire, including the Greeks, referred to and considered themselves Romans until the very end. The empire itself was polyglot as it always was, but the dominant language was Greek. Thus, while the “Middle Ages” or medieval period happened in the west, which was still backward, that was not the case in the east, in what in fact was the bulk of the empire, which continued a thriving, but heavily Christianized civilization. Thus, in the year 1000 Constantinople had a population of over a million people. The original Roman Empire was far better at practical things, particularly organization, administration, functional engineering, etc. than the quarrelsome Greeks, who otherwise brilliantly developed and dominated culture, art, science, philosophy, etc. Romans provided the critical stability, legal and social infrastructure that was previously lacking in an otherwise largely Greek world that had been established by Alexander and his successors. As a result, Roman law, justice and organization provided the framework which sustained an otherwise largely Greek cultural entity. The empire would not have fallen had it not been for the Fourth Crusade (1202–1204) which, instead of going to Jerusalem to fight Muslims attacked other Christians via Venetian ships and encouragement. The barbarian Knights/Crusaders literally destroyed the city of Constantinople, pillaging and worse, burning down much of the city while the Venetians, at least having some artistic sense, carted off a lot of treasures that you still see in St. Marks to this day. The crusaders took over what was left of the city setting up their own “empire” for a few decades until the Romans finally reclaimed it, but in a much-weakened state. Thus, by the time the Turks finally conquered the city in 1453 with new long-range cannons, there were only about 50,000 people left there. That is when the Roman Empire finally fell, in its Greco-Roman-Christian incarnation. Given true history then, if the empire hadn’t fallen it is quite possible that Greek would still be the common language, you might be speaking it, and the European world would be very different. The “old” nations of Europe after all, have only existed for around five centuries. They really ascended after the fall of the City and the “renaissance” that followed, (another retroactively coined term), instilled to a considerable extent by Greek refugee scholars who fled to the Italian city-states, which welcomed then as teachers, given their thirst for knowledge and ancient manuscripts. Many other things would be different, starting with religion. In the empire the church was subordinate to the Emperor, and less powerful than in the west, where given the power vacuum, the Bishop of Rome, or Pope, was able to claim supremacy. Consequently, if the empire had continued the church would not have had so much power, and it is likely there would never have been a Protestant Reformation. Regions would have had their own Patriarchs. There is no way to know how geography would have taken shape, given uncertainty as to how far the empire might have reached, or how competent it would have been, but at its maximum it could have stretched over all of Europe. Alternatively, it could have been smaller, as it continued to fend of endless barbarian invasions from the east, allowing other powers to emerge in the west anyway, but possibly without the virulent nationalism that eventually developed and led to catastrophic wars and mass murder in the last century. Much would depend on whether the empire could regain Italy, which was essential to the emergence of modern Europe. (In 1500 Italy was richer than all of western Europe combined and more culturally advanced). Since it was then divided into competing city-states in the fashion of ancient Greece, that might have transpired if the empire was relatively free from barbarian invasions. Slavs, at least in the south were already being absorbed before the fall of the empire and thus would likely still be integrated. Unknowns are how the Russians, or more importantly the Germans might have emerged. But generally, the empire had always done a great job of absorbing and integrating other peoples, until the rise of Islam. If the empire had remained strong it is unlikely that the Arabs would have conquered what was then European Christian north Africa and Egypt, or even much of what is now called the “middle east,” which would have remained Christian and Roman, linked to the west via Constantinople. The empire took the brunt of Muslim invasion, thus protecting the west for centuries, and if not for the Fourth Crusade could have grown stronger and more powerful and Europe would not have been threatened or invaded. In addition, Persian culture might still exist, possibly as yet another empire. Greek rationalism did not disappear as the church in the east largely reconciled itself with it and focused on spiritual matters. Consequently, the church would not have been able to significantly thwart scientific progress. Europe, including a good portion of the east would still dominate the world. and remain centered in Constantinople. They would likely still have found the Americas, but development might have been different, possibly without African slavery, among other things. The culture would be more advanced and sophisticated, but economic growth might not be as robust, given a different emphasis and outlook, and without a “Protestant ethic” but rather a sort of merchant mentality. Higher education might not have been found in universities as we know them, but rather closer to the academic format of the ancient world, more focused on the development of the mind and learning. Ultimately we cannot know because of vicissitudes of one-man rule. There can be a great ruler and then a terrible ruler. You can have a Marcus Aurelius or a Caligula. So given different personalities there is no way to know, and that can be precarious and lead to instability or conflict until someone else consolidates power. What we can learn clearly from history is the less power we surrender to others over us the better off we are. Finally, the Fourth Crusade was clearly the worst disaster in western history even beyond World War I if only because the latter might never have happened if the empire hadn’t fallen. Such a general and vague question can lead to endless possibilities and alternatives, but in the end all that is left is what actually happened.

items.model_answer:
If the Roman Empire had never fallen, the single biggest difference in our world today would likely be the absence of a fragmented Europe and, as a result, a very different path toward modern nation-states, global colonization, and even democracy.

First, political continuity would have transformed Europe. After Rome’s collapse in the West (5th century), Europe fractured into competing kingdoms, which over centuries evolved into nations like France, England, Spain, and Germany. That fragmentation fostered intense competition—military, economic, and technological—which later fueled exploration, empire-building, and industrialization. If Rome had remained politically unified and administratively effective, Europe might have developed more like a vast, centralized imperial state, similar in some ways to imperial China. Modern nationalism might have emerged much later or in weaker form. Instead of dozens of sovereign European states, we might have inherited a large Roman commonwealth spanning much of Europe, North Africa, and parts of the Middle East.

Second, religion and culture would likely look different. Christianity spread partly through Rome’s infrastructure, but the fall of the Western Empire allowed the Church to become a separate, stabilizing authority. If Rome had remained strong, the Church might have stayed more tightly controlled by imperial power, reducing the chances of a deep divide between secular and religious authority. The Protestant Reformation, which depended on political fragmentation and local rulers defying Rome (both papal and imperial), might not have happened—or would have taken a very different form. A more religiously unified Europe could have emerged, or alternatively, a more tightly regulated imperial Christianity.

Third, technological and economic development might have followed a slower but steadier trajectory. The early medieval period saw economic contraction after Rome’s fall, but that collapse also reset systems and eventually encouraged new forms of organization, such as feudalism and later capitalism. A continuous Roman Empire might have preserved large estates, slave-based labor systems, and centralized trade networks for longer. That could have delayed the rise of decentralized markets and industrial capitalism. On the other hand, sustained imperial infrastructure—roads, legal systems, trade networks—might have accelerated economic integration across Europe and the Mediterranean, possibly leading to earlier large-scale urbanization and bureaucratic governance.

Fourth, global colonization might have unfolded differently. The European “Age of Exploration” was driven by rival states seeking trade routes and imperial advantage. A unified Roman superstate might have had less incentive for risky maritime competition—or, conversely, it might have launched state-sponsored expansion on an even larger scale. The Americas might have been colonized not by competing Spanish, English, and French empires, but by a single Roman imperial authority, spreading Latin language and Roman law even more uniformly across the globe.

Finally, modern political ideas would likely be altered. Concepts such as constitutionalism, sovereignty, and nationhood emerged from Europe’s medieval fragmentation and later conflicts like the Thirty Years’ War. A continuous empire might have normalized centralized bureaucratic rule for centuries. Modern democracy could either have emerged earlier through imperial reforms (similar to gradual expansions of Roman citizenship) or much later, if imperial authority remained dominant and resistant to political pluralism.

In short, if the Roman Empire had never fallen, we would probably live in a world shaped less by competing nation-states and more by long-term imperial continuity. Languages, borders, religions, and political systems would be more unified across Europe and perhaps beyond. The modern world—defined by nationalism, global rivalries, and diverse political systems—would likely be replaced by something more centralized, more culturally continuous, and possibly less politically fragmented, for better or worse.

items.question: What If the Roman Empire still exists? How different would the world be now?
human_answers: As always, the first thing we need to think about is the population and land of the newly recreated Roman Empire. First of all, a total of 53 Countries would lose all or some of their land to the empire over a total of a gargantuan 6,330,000 square kilometres but it would be only the 7th Largest Country in the world being just ahead of India (3,287,263 square kilometres), but remaining well behind other massive countries like Australia (7,692,024 square kilometres), and Brazil (8,515,767 square kilometres). As well as a huge land area, the Roman Empire would also have an immense population of around 710,000,000. This is huge and would be enough to put it in 3rd place, in terms of population, being well ahead of the United States (328,200,000) but also remaining well behind India (1.381 Billion), and China (1.398 Billion). Next, the Capital City would be quite debatable as the Roman Empire had a few historical capitals but the most likely choice would be Rome as it was the first historical Roman Capital and is already the capital of modern-day Italy. However, Rome has a puny population and wouldn't even make it in the top 10 largest cities in the new empire! The largest city would be Cairo, in Egypt, with a massive population of 21,500,000 compared to Rome's tiny 3,800,000. Here would be the top 5 largest urban areas in the empires. As well as being a land juggernaut, the Roman Empire would also be an extremely prosperous nation with a nominal GDP of a massive $16 Trillion mainly because of the high GDP countries of the United Kingdom, France, and Italy being absorbed into the empire. This huge GDP would put it in 3rd place being well ahead of other wealthy nations like Japan ($4.85 Trillion) and Germany ($3.86 Trillion), however, it would be just behind China ($16.64 Trillion) and again well behind the United States ($20.81 Trillion). The GDP Per Capita wouldn't be so impressive though due to the poor areas of Iraq, Armenia, Libya, and Syria. As a result, the GDP per Capita would stand at an estimated $22,535 which is reasonable but is still quite a low value. If the Roman Empire still existed today, the modern world would be radically different in politics, religion, language, and global power structures—but how different depends on what “still exists” means. The Roman Empire could not have survived unchanged from antiquity; it would have had to evolve. So the more realistic scenario is not legions in sandals ruling Europe, but a continuous Roman state that gradually modernized instead of collapsing in the West in the 5th century.

Politically, Europe would likely be far more unified. The fall of Rome led to fragmented kingdoms, feudalism, and eventually the nation-state system. If Rome had endured, Western Europe might have developed as a centralized imperial federation rather than separate countries like France, Germany, Spain, and Italy. National identities might be weaker, replaced by a broader Roman civic identity. The European Union might be unnecessary because political unity would already exist in some form.

Religion would also look different. Christianity became dominant partly through the Roman imperial structure, but the collapse of the Western Empire strengthened the independent political power of the Papacy. If Rome had remained politically unified, the Church might never have gained the same autonomous authority. The Protestant Reformation may have unfolded differently—or not at all—if imperial governance had maintained tighter religious cohesion or enforced religious pluralism earlier.

Linguistically, Latin might have remained the dominant administrative and cultural language across Europe. Instead of French, Spanish, Portuguese, and Italian developing into fully distinct national languages, they might resemble regional dialects within a standardized imperial Latin. English might be very different too, since the Germanic migrations into Britain were partly enabled by Roman withdrawal. Without that withdrawal, England might be Latin-speaking.

Globally, colonialism would likely have taken a different form. A unified Roman Empire with Mediterranean naval dominance could have led early transoceanic exploration as a centralized project, rather than through competition between Spain, Portugal, England, and France. The Americas might have been incorporated as imperial provinces rather than as colonies of rival nation-states. Global politics today might revolve around a few mega-empires rather than dozens of sovereign nations.

Economically and technologically, continuity might have accelerated development. The collapse of Western Roman infrastructure led to centuries of reduced urbanization and economic contraction in parts of Europe. If imperial systems of roads, trade networks, taxation, and law had persisted and modernized, industrialization might have begun earlier—or at least more smoothly. On the other hand, centralized stability can also suppress innovation if it discourages competition.

The biggest difference might be conceptual: the modern idea of sovereign nation-states might never have emerged. Our current international system, shaped by post-Roman fragmentation and later treaties like Westphalia, might instead be a world of enduring imperial polities. Citizenship might be tied to imperial legal status rather than nationality.

In short, a surviving Roman Empire would likely mean a more politically unified Europe, a stronger continuity of Latin culture, a different religious balance, altered patterns of colonization, and a global order built around large imperial structures rather than nation-states. The modern world would still have technology, democracy movements, and globalization—but filtered through a two‑thousand‑year-old evolving imperial framework rather than the patchwork of nations we know today.

items.question: What If the Roman Empire survived into the 21st century?
human_answers: A surviving Roman Empire in the 21st century would reshape politics, culture, technology diffusion, religion, law, and global power structures. Below is a compact, structured scenario sketching plausible continuities, ruptures, and systemic consequences while anchoring changes in realistic mechanisms (institutional inertia, technological adoption, conquest limits, cultural assimilation). Core-continuities and institutions Imperial continuity: The Empire preserves imperial institutions—an emperor (or imperial council), provincial administration, legions as core armed forces, and a bureaucratic elite—adapted over centuries into flexible, meritocratic civil service and imperial parliament/assemblies to manage scale. Roman law as global lingua franca: Codified law (an evolved Corpus Juris) becomes the legal foundation across the Empire and, by prestige and trade, a dominant model beyond it; concepts like property rights, contracts, corporate forms, and administrative law are widespread. Urbanism and infrastructure: Roman urban planning, roads, aqueduct successors, ports, and integrated logistics persist and modernize. Dense metropolitan networks across the Mediterranean, Western and parts of Central Europe, North Africa, Anatolia and the Levant remain economic cores. Multilingual administration: Latin remains the imperial legal-administrative language but coexists with vernaculars (Greek, Punic, Syriac, Germanic, Celtic, Berber dialects). A strong tradition of bilingual or trilingual elites exists. Geopolitics and territorial shape Core territories: The Empire holds the Mediterranean rim (Iberia to Levant), much of North Africa, Italy, the Balkans, Anatolia, parts of Central Europe and possibly Britain as a client or integrated province—boundaries adjusted by later contingencies. Successor or extra-European states: Outside the imperial ambit, consolidated polities (a unified Frankish realm, Slavic federations, Islamic caliphates expanded differently, and later colonial states in the Americas, sub-Saharan Africa, and East Asia) create a multipolar world. The Empire competes with and sometimes partners with maritime powers. Imperial fragmentation avoided or mitigated: Rather than a single uninterrupted polity by 2025, the Empire is likely a federated imperial system—suffragan kingdoms, semi-autonomous provinces, and imperial dynasties alternating with elective mechanisms—preventing collapse while allowing regional autonomy. Religion and ideology Religion pluralism anchored in Roman legalism: Early Christianity, or a pluralized Roman state religion that incorporated Christianity, remains influential but subject to imperial regulation. Religious plurality (Judaism, localized pagan survivals, later Islam and Eastern religions) exists with legal frameworks for toleration and civic participation. Secularization pathways: Enlightenment-like movements and commercial modernization produce robust secular administrative norms by the 19th–20th centuries; an imperial secular public sphere coexists with powerful religious institutions. Economy and technology Industrialization: The Empire experiences industrial revolutions driven by integrated markets, stable property law, and urban demand. State investment in infrastructure and military spurs rail, steam, later electric and digital technologies. Industrial centers cluster where Roman urban networks were densest. Trade networks: The Empire’s Mediterranean-centered trade orientation evolves into global commerce via long-distance maritime routes; imperial ports become hubs connecting to Atlantic and Indian Ocean circuits. Maritime technology advances compete with and eventually match Atlantic powers. Banking and corporate forms: Advanced Roman legal corporations (sodalitates, societates) evolve into joint-stock companies, central banking, and imperial-chartered trading companies. Rome-centric financial systems influence global credit norms. Military and diplomacy Professionalized legions: Legions transform into modern, well-funded standing forces with combined-arms doctrine, naval fleets, and expeditionary capabilities; conscription and recruitment adapt to demographic realities. Gunpowder, industrial warfare, nuclear age: The Empire participates fully in the technological military revolution. Its strategic choices (naval investments, alliances, nuclear development) shape 20th-century geopolitics. Balance with other great powers prevents unlimited expansion. Diplomacy: Roman legal diplomacy—treaties, client states, and provincial autonomy—produces layered influence: direct rule where feasible, client kingdoms and protectorates elsewhere, and trade-dominant zones beyond. Culture, identity, and languages Roman identity as civic, not ethnic: Imperial civic identity (civis Romana) emphasizes legal status, obligations, and urban participation rather than ethnicity. Cultural assimilation is patchy; local identities persist under Roman civic frameworks. Latin’s evolution: Vulgar Latin branches into multiple Romance languages with imperial Latin retained for law, liturgy, and academia. Greek remains influential in eastern provinces; multilingualism is common in elites. Arts and sciences: Patronage systems shift from emperors and aristocrats to universities, public institutions, and corporate sponsors. A continuous tradition of Roman engineering and medicine blends with global scientific developments. Colonialism and global expansion Atlantic exploration: Roman maritime institutions and entrepreneurial elites engage in Atlantic exploration. Depending on timing and internal politics, Rome might participate in early colonial ventures or be competed against by independent maritime republics and emergent Atlantic states. Americas and Asia: If Rome delays Atlantic expansion, independent colonial empires arise (Portuguese/Spanish-analogs, Dutch/English-analogs), producing a patchwork of territories. Alternatively, Roman-chartered companies acquire colonies, producing a Roman-speaking settler/merchant presence in the Americas or parts of Africa. Non-European contacts: Sustained contact with Chinese, Indian, and later Pacific polities leads to trade, technology transfer, and complex diplomacy rather than simple conquest. Science, education, and bureaucracy State-sponsored technical education: Roman practicality produces strong engineering schools and imperial academies; public health and civil engineering remain priorities. Literacy rates among urban populations are higher than in many historical analogs. Administrative continuity fosters record-keeping, statistics, and early modern state capacities (census, taxation, public works), accelerating institutional modernization. Possible alternative 20th–21st century dynamics Different alignments in world wars or great-power wars: If imperial fragmentation is limited, large-scale continental wars might occur between the Empire and other consolidated powers. The Empire’s size and resources could prevent dominance by any single non-imperial power, producing a multipolar 20th century with competing blocs. Cold-war analogues: Ideological divides (imperial corporatism vs. revolutionary republics, religious empires vs. secular federations) could create bipolar tensions that include spheres of influence, proxy conflicts, intelligence competition, and arms races including nuclear weapons. European integration replaced by imperial federalization: Instead of EU-style nation-states, regional federal assemblies and an imperial senate coordinate economic policy, standards, and internal mobility at an imperial scale. Society and daily life in 21st-century Roman Empire Urban-rural divide: Highly urbanized imperial cores with advanced services contrast with peripheral provinces with varying development. Provincial capitals are modern metros with Roman street plans, monumental continuity, and modern skyscrapers intermingled with ancient fabric. Civic rituals and symbolism: Imperial ceremonies, legal oaths, and municipal collegia persist as public rituals; imperial monuments and restored ancient sites are central to civic pride and tourism. Social mobility: Legal pathways (citizenship-by-service, trade-based citizenship, imperial grants) enable mobility. Aristocratic families persist but compete with bureaucratic meritocrats and industrial capitalists. Long-term cultural impact beyond the Empire Legal and bureaucratic export: Roman-derived legal codes and administrative practices diffuse globally through trade, education, and colonialism, shaping modern governance worldwide. Architectural and engineering legacy: Roman building methods evolve into modern construction norms in the imperial sphere; global architecture shows stronger classical continuity. Intellectual tradition: A continuous stream of classical scholarship, merged with scientific revolutions, produces different emphases in philosophy, law, and humanistic studies—less romantic nationalism, more civic-universalist discourse. Summary — plausible consequences The 21st-century world would be multipolar but strongly influenced by a Rome-centered legal, administrative, and infrastructural complex. Technological and industrial modernity develops within Roman institutional forms rather than in nation-state molds. Colonial and global expansions produce complex interactions with Americas, Asia, and Africa; outcomes depend crucially on early maritime strategy and whether Rome embraced or ceded Atlantic exploration. Socially and culturally, a Roman civic identity coexists with strong local cultures and multilingualism; legal-civic institutions and urban infrastructure are the Empire’s durable strengths. Global politics would differ in alignments, ideologies, and the balance of maritime vs. continental power, but modern technologies (industrialization, nuclear weapons, digital networks) and economic forces remain drivers—shaping a recognizable but distinct modern world. Examples and analogues Byzantine survival gives a model: An eastern Roman continuity (Byzantium) demonstrates how Roman law, bureaucracy, and urbanism can endure, adapt to new religions and languages, and project power for centuries. Ottoman adaptation shows how a premodern empire modernizes militarily and administratively under internal reform pressures. British imperial experience illustrates how an empire with maritime orientation, legal export, and industrial base shapes world systems—transpose British mechanisms onto Roman institutions for multiple plausible outcomes. This scenario emphasizes institutional adaptability, legal continuity, and urban infrastructure as the key mechanisms enabling a Roman Empire’s survival and modernization, producing a 21st century both recognizably Roman and reshaped by global technological and political currents.
